problems.title: A polarization gradient carries volume charge
problems.objective: Differentiate a nonuniform polarization, include both material faces, and verify neutrality without losing the outward-normal signs.
problems.statement: A dielectric slab occupies $-a<x<a$ and has polarization $\mathbf P(x)=P_0(x/a)\hat{\mathbf x}$ inside and zero outside. There is no free charge. Find the bound volume charge density and the bound surface charge density on both faces. Integrate all bound charge per unit transverse area and verify the result.
problems.strategy: Differentiate the polarization only where the material law is defined, then evaluate the two boundary faces with their own outward normals. A per-area charge sum checks the volume and surface signs together.
hints: Differentiate only the interior field when computing $\rho_b$.
Write the outward normal separately at $x=a$ and $x=-a$.
Compare the integrated volume charge with the sum of the two face charges.
problems.solution: Inside the slab, $\rho_b=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf P=-dP_x/dx=-P_0/a$. At $x=a$, the outward normal is $+\hat{\mathbf x}$, so $\sigma_b=\mathbf P\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=P_0$. At $x=-a$, both $\mathbf P=-P_0\hat{\mathbf x}$ and $\hat{\mathbf n}=-\hat{\mathbf x}$, hence $\sigma_b=P_0$ there as well. The volume contribution per unit area is $(-P_0/a)(2a)=-2P_0$, while the two faces contribute $2P_0$. The total is zero, as required for polarization made by displacing bound charge rather than adding net charge.
rubricCriteria: Obtains $\rho_b=-P_0/a$ in the slab.
Finds $\sigma_b=P_0$ on each material face using the correct normals.
Shows explicitly that the net bound charge per unit area vanishes.

commonErrors.description: Treats both outward normals as positive x.
commonErrors.consequence: One surface sign is assigned from coordinates rather than from the material boundary orientation.

commonErrors.description: Counts only the face at positive x.
commonErrors.consequence: The volume charge then appears to violate neutrality because a physical boundary contribution is missing.

problems.flawedProof: The polarization points toward negative $x$ at the left face, so that face has $\sigma_b=-P_0$. The two surface charges cancel and the remaining volume charge is a real net charge.

problems.title: Uniform polarization moves charge to opposite faces
problems.objective: Use oriented surface normals to distinguish the two face charges of a uniformly polarized finite slab.
problems.statement: A finite dielectric block is uniformly polarized as $\mathbf P=P_0\hat{\mathbf z}$. Its top and bottom faces have area $A$ and outward normals $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ and $-\hat{\mathbf z}$. Find all bound charge densities and the bound charge on each of those faces. Explain why the side faces and volume carry none.
problems.strategy: Begin with the zero divergence of a spatially uniform polarization. Map the top, bottom, and side normals separately so the resulting face charges can be checked for net neutrality.
hints: A spatially constant vector field has zero divergence.
Evaluate $\mathbf P\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$ on each orientation, not just its magnitude.
Normals to the side faces lie in the horizontal plane.
problems.solution: Uniform polarization has zero divergence, so $\rho_b=0$. On the top face, $\sigma_b=\mathbf P\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=P_0$ and $Q_{\rm top}=P_0A$. On the bottom face, $\sigma_b=-P_0$ and $Q_{\rm bottom}=-P_0A$. Every side normal is perpendicular to $\hat{\mathbf z}$, so its surface density is zero. The opposite face charges sum to zero and represent separated bound charge.
rubricCriteria: Identifies zero bound volume charge.
Reports $+P_0$ and $-P_0$ on the top and bottom faces with charges $\pm P_0A$.
Explains the absence of side charge and the zero total charge.

commonErrors.description: Assigns positive bound charge to both horizontal faces.
commonErrors.consequence: Ignoring the bottom outward normal creates a spurious net bound charge.

commonErrors.description: Uses polarization magnitude as a volume density.
commonErrors.consequence: Polarization has charge per area units, and only its divergence produces volume charge.

problems.flawedProof: Uniform polarization has zero volume charge and no side-face charge. Because both horizontal faces belong to the same block, assign $\sigma_b=+P_0$ to each of them, so both carry $+P_0A$.

problems.title: Radial polarization produces a compensating shell charge
problems.objective: Compute bound volume and surface charge for a spherical polarization field and close the global charge balance.
problems.statement: A dielectric sphere of radius $R$ has $\mathbf P=kr\hat{\mathbf r}$ for $r<R$ and zero outside, where $k$ is constant. Find $\rho_b$, the surface density at $r=R$, and the total bound charge from each contribution.
problems.strategy: Use the spherical divergence including its radial Jacobian, and treat the cutoff at the sphere surface as a separate source. Integrating the bulk and shell densities exposes the compensating charge exactly.
hints: Apply the spherical divergence formula to $f(r)=kr$.
At $r=R$, the material outward normal is $\hat{\mathbf r}$.
Integrate the constant volume density over the sphere before comparing charges.
problems.solution: For a radial field, $\nabla\cdot(f\hat{\mathbf r})=r^{-2}d(r^2f)/dr$. With $f=kr$, the divergence is $3k$, so $\rho_b=-3k$. At the surface, $\sigma_b=\mathbf P(R)\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}=kR$. Thus $Q_{\rm vol}=(-3k)(4\pi R^3/3)=-4\pi kR^3$ and $Q_{\rm surf}=(kR)(4\pi R^2)=4\pi kR^3$. Their sum is zero.
rubricCriteria: Derives $\rho_b=-3k$.
Derives $\sigma_b=kR$ and both total charges.
Verifies cancellation with correct dimensions and signs.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates only $kr$ and obtains $\rho_b=-k$.
commonErrors.consequence: The spherical Jacobian is omitted, undercounting the divergence by a factor of three.

commonErrors.description: Omits the discontinuity at the sphere boundary.
commonErrors.consequence: The compensating bound surface charge is lost.

problems.flawedProof: Differentiate only the scalar coefficient of $kr\hat{\mathbf r}$, obtaining $\rho_b=-k$. The outer face still has $\sigma_b=kR$, so its charge is $4\pi kR^3$ while the volume charge is $-4\pi kR^3/3$.

problems.title: A polarized sphere has a measurable dipole moment
problems.objective: Relate a uniform polarization to its total dipole moment and evaluate a far-axis field numerically.
problems.statement: A sphere of radius $2.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ is uniformly polarized with $P_0=3.00\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$ along $+z$. Find its electric dipole moment. Using the dipole approximation, find the axial electric field magnitude at $z=0.500\,\mathrm m$. State the small parameter controlling the approximation.
problems.strategy: Form the dipole moment from polarization times volume before inserting any numbers. Convert all lengths to SI units, apply the axial far-field expression, and use the radius-to-distance ratio to audit the approximation.
hints: Convert the radius to metres before forming the volume.
Uniform $\mathbf P$ factors out of the volume integral.
Use $R/z$, rather than $R$ alone, to assess the far-field approximation.
problems.solution: The dipole moment of uniform polarization is $\mathbf p=\int\mathbf P\,dV=P_0(4\pi R^3/3)\hat{\mathbf z}$. With $R=0.0200\,\mathrm m$, $p=1.01\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{C\,m}$. The axial dipole field is $E_z=(1/(4\pi\epsilon_0))(2p/z^3)$, which gives $E_z=14.5\,\mathrm{V/m}$ toward $+z$. The expansion parameter is $R/z=0.0400$, so omitted multipoles are strongly suppressed.
rubricCriteria: Computes $p=1.01\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{C\,m}$.
Computes $E_z=14.5\,\mathrm{V/m}$ with the correct direction.
Identifies $R/z=0.0400$ as the relevant scale ratio.

commonErrors.description: Uses the sphere surface area instead of its volume.
commonErrors.consequence: The result retains charge rather than dipole-moment dimensions.

commonErrors.description: Uses the equatorial dipole coefficient on the axis.
commonErrors.consequence: The axial field is underestimated by a factor of two and its geometry is misidentified.

problems.flawedProof: Treat polarization as dipole moment per surface area, giving $p=4\pi R^2P_0$. Then use the supplied axial formula unchanged: $E_{\rm axis}=2p/(4\pi\epsilon_0z^3)$.

problems.title: An internal polarization jump is a charged interface
problems.objective: Derive the bound sheet charge at a material-material boundary with one declared normal and reconcile the two face conventions.
problems.statement: Two polarized media meet at $z=0$. In medium 1, below the plane, $\mathbf P_1=P_1\hat{\mathbf z}$; in medium 2, above it, $\mathbf P_2=P_2\hat{\mathbf z}$. Take the interface normal $\hat{\mathbf n}_{12}=+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Find the net bound sheet charge at the interface by adding the charge on each material face, and express it as a jump formula.
permittedResults: $\sigma_b=\mathbf P\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}_{\rm out}$ on each material face
problems.strategy: Declare one interface normal from material 1 to material 2, while retaining opposite outward normals for the two material faces. Compute both face densities first; only afterward compress their sum into a polarization jump.
hints: The two materials have opposite outward normals at their common boundary.
Add the two face densities before compressing the answer into a jump.
A jump formula is meaningful only after its normal direction is declared.
problems.solution: The outward normal of medium 1 at its upper face is $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, giving $\sigma_{b1}=P_1$. The outward normal of medium 2 at its lower face is $-\hat{\mathbf z}$, giving $\sigma_{b2}=-P_2$. Hence the net interface density is $\sigma_b=P_1-P_2=(\mathbf P_1-\mathbf P_2)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}_{12}$. Reversing the declared jump normal swaps the labels and leaves the physical sum unchanged when the formula is transformed consistently.
rubricCriteria: Finds the separate face charges $P_1$ and $-P_2$.
Obtains $\sigma_b=P_1-P_2$ for the stated normal.
Explains normal-reversal consistency rather than treating the sign as intrinsic.

commonErrors.description: Uses the same outward normal for both materials.
commonErrors.consequence: The interface charge becomes a sum instead of the physical difference.

commonErrors.description: Writes a jump without naming its orientation.
commonErrors.consequence: The sign cannot be interpreted or compared with boundary conditions.

problems.flawedProof: Use $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ as the outward normal for both material faces. Their densities are then $P_1$ and $P_2$, so the net bound interface charge is $P_1+P_2$.

problems.title: Gauss law for D isolates free line charge
problems.objective: Use cylindrical symmetry to find displacement and electric fields in a homogeneous dielectric while separating free and bound charge.
problems.statement: An infinite free line charge $\lambda_f$ lies on the axis of a homogeneous linear dielectric with permittivity $\epsilon$. Find $\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf E$ for $r>0$. If $\epsilon=\kappa\epsilon_0$, find the bound charge per unit length concentrated on an infinitesimal cylindrical cavity around the line.
permittedResults: $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$ in a linear isotropic dielectric
problems.strategy: Let free line charge determine displacement flux without mixing in polarization charge. Convert displacement to the field in each region, then recover polarization and use the cavity normal to verify the screened electric source.
hints: Apply the flux law to $\mathbf D$, whose source is free charge.
Use $\mathbf P=(\epsilon-\epsilon_0)\mathbf E$ after finding the fields.
The dielectric outward normal at an inner cavity is opposite the radial coordinate direction.
problems.solution: Cylindrical symmetry gives $\mathbf D=D_r(r)\hat{\mathbf r}$. A Gaussian cylinder yields $D_r(2\pi rL)=\lambda_fL$, so $\mathbf D=\lambda_f\hat{\mathbf r}/(2\pi r)$. Therefore $\mathbf E=\mathbf D/\epsilon$. In the dielectric, $\mathbf P=(\epsilon-\epsilon_0)\mathbf E=(1-1/\kappa)\mathbf D$. On the inner wall of a small material cavity the dielectric outward normal points toward the axis, so the bound charge per length is $\lambda_b=-(1-1/\kappa)\lambda_f$. The combined source seen by E is $\lambda_f/\kappa$.
rubricCriteria: Derives $\mathbf D=\lambda_f\hat{\mathbf r}/(2\pi r)$.
Converts D to E using the material permittivity.
Finds $\lambda_b=-(1-1/\kappa)\lambda_f$ with the cavity-normal sign.

commonErrors.description: Uses total charge as the source of D.
commonErrors.consequence: The constitutive separation between free and bound charge is erased.

commonErrors.description: Uses the outer-surface normal on the inner cavity wall.
commonErrors.consequence: The bound line charge acquires the wrong sign and would enhance rather than screen the free charge.

problems.flawedProof: Because the dielectric contains bound charge, use total rather than free charge in the displacement flux: $D_r2\pi rL=(\lambda_f+\lambda_b)L$. With the inward cavity normal, take $\lambda_b=-(1-1/\kappa)\lambda_f$ and hence $D_r=\lambda_f/(2\pi\kappa r)$.

problems.title: A free sheet fixes the normal jump of D
problems.objective: Apply the oriented displacement boundary condition and distinguish it from tangential electric-field continuity.
problems.statement: Media 1 and 2 meet at a plane with unit normal $\hat{\mathbf n}$ pointing from 1 to 2. A free surface charge density $\sigma_f$ lies on the interface. Derive the electrostatic conditions for the normal component of $\mathbf D$ and the tangential component of $\mathbf E$. Then evaluate $D_{2n}$ when $D_{1n}=2.00\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$ and $\sigma_f=-0.500\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$.
problems.strategy: Derive the normal displacement jump with an oriented pillbox and the tangential electric condition with a shrinking loop. Apply the signed numerical sheet charge only after those vector conventions are fixed.
hints: Keep the pillbox normal aligned with the declared direction from medium 1 to medium 2.
The loop law constrains tangential $\mathbf E$, not tangential $\mathbf D$.
Add the signed free density to the side-1 normal component.
problems.solution: A thin pillbox gives $(\mathbf D_2-\mathbf D_1)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=\sigma_f$. A thin rectangular loop and $\nabla\times\mathbf E=0$ give $\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\mathbf E_2-\mathbf E_1)=\mathbf0$. Thus $D_{2n}=D_{1n}+\sigma_f=1.50\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$. The normal E component need not be continuous because the constitutive factors can differ, and the normal D component is continuous only when free surface charge vanishes.
rubricCriteria: Derives both oriented interface conditions.
Computes $D_{2n}=1.50\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$.
States which other components may jump and why.

commonErrors.description: Sets the normal D components equal despite nonzero free charge.
commonErrors.consequence: The pillbox flux fails to account for its enclosed free sheet.

commonErrors.description: Applies tangential continuity to D.
commonErrors.consequence: A constitutive field is substituted for the curl-free electric field.

problems.flawedProof: The normal component of $\mathbf D$ is continuous across every dielectric interface, even with a free sheet, so $D_{2n}=D_{1n}=2.00\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$. The tangential electric field remains continuous by the electrostatic loop law.

problems.title: Two dielectrics in series share D, not E
problems.objective: Solve a layered parallel-plate capacitor from free-charge boundary data and compute voltage and capacitance.
problems.statement: A parallel-plate capacitor of area $A$ contains dielectric 1 of thickness $d_1$ and permittivity $\epsilon_1$ and dielectric 2 of thickness $d_2$ and permittivity $\epsilon_2$, stacked normal to the plates. The plates carry free charges $\pm Q$ and fringing is neglected. Find $\mathbf D$, the field in each layer, the voltage magnitude, and the capacitance.
problems.strategy: Use the electrode free charge to establish one common normal displacement through the stack. Translate it into two fields, add their voltage drops, and invert the result for the series capacitance.
hints: Use the plate free charge to set $D_n=Q/A$.
Convert the same displacement into a different electric field in each medium.
Add the two potential drops before taking the ratio Q over V.
problems.solution: There is no free charge at the internal interface, so the normal displacement is constant: $D=Q/A$. Each field is $E_i=D/\epsilon_i=Q/(A\epsilon_i)$. The voltage is $V=E_1d_1+E_2d_2=(Q/A)(d_1/\epsilon_1+d_2/\epsilon_2)$. Hence $C=Q/V=A/(d_1/\epsilon_1+d_2/\epsilon_2)$. The result is the series combination of the two layer capacitances and reduces to $\epsilon A/(d_1+d_2)$ when the permittivities are equal.
rubricCriteria: Finds common $D=Q/A$ and both electric fields.
Adds the layer voltage drops with correct dimensions.
Obtains $C=A/(d_1/\epsilon_1+d_2/\epsilon_2)$ and checks an equal-material limit.

commonErrors.description: Assumes the electric field is the same in both layers.
commonErrors.consequence: The normal displacement condition is confused with electric-field continuity.

commonErrors.description: Adds layer capacitances directly.
commonErrors.consequence: Stacking along the field direction is a series, not parallel, geometry.

problems.flawedProof: Electric-field continuity makes $E_1=E_2=E$. Taking $E=Q/[A(\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2)]$ gives $V=E(d_1+d_2)$ and therefore $C=A(\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2)/(d_1+d_2)$.

problems.title: A point charge in a dielectric is screened by bound charge
problems.objective: Find D, E, and the induced bound source for a free point charge in an infinite homogeneous dielectric.
problems.statement: A free point charge $q$ is embedded in an infinite homogeneous linear dielectric with relative permittivity $\kappa$. Find $\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf E$ for $r>0$. By integrating polarization over a small spherical cavity around the charge, determine the induced bound charge associated with the source.
problems.strategy: Start from displacement flux sourced by the unscreened free point charge. Express polarization as a fraction of displacement, orient the inner material boundary inward, and compare the resulting bound charge with the effective electric source.
hints: Use the free point charge, not the screened total, in the displacement flux.
Express $\mathbf P$ as a fraction of $\mathbf D$.
For a cavity, the material normal points into the removed ball.
problems.solution: Spherical symmetry and free-charge Gauss law give $\mathbf D=q\hat{\mathbf r}/(4\pi r^2)$. Thus $\mathbf E=q\hat{\mathbf r}/(4\pi\kappa\epsilon_0r^2)$ and $\mathbf P=(1-1/\kappa)\mathbf D$. The material outward normal on the inner wall of a small cavity is $-\hat{\mathbf r}$, so $Q_b=\oint\mathbf P\cdot(-\hat{\mathbf r})\,dA=-(1-1/\kappa)q$. Therefore the effective total source for E is $q+Q_b=q/\kappa$.
rubricCriteria: Derives the radial displacement and screened electric field.
Finds $Q_b=-(1-1/\kappa)q$.
Checks that the net source inferred from E is $q/\kappa$.

commonErrors.description: Places the factor of kappa in D.
commonErrors.consequence: The displacement flux no longer equals the enclosed free charge.

commonErrors.description: Uses a positive cavity normal and obtains positive screening charge.
commonErrors.consequence: The polarization response would reinforce a positive free source instead of screening it.

problems.flawedProof: Screening reduces the displacement itself to $\mathbf D=q\hat{\mathbf r}/(4\pi\kappa r^2)$. Using the inward material normal then gives a negative cavity charge from the resulting polarization.

problems.title: Free charge on a dielectric sphere fixes a piecewise field
problems.objective: Solve a concentric dielectric-vacuum boundary problem and audit free and bound surface charge separately.
problems.statement: A dielectric sphere of radius $R$ and permittivity $\epsilon=\kappa\epsilon_0$ contains a free point charge $q$ at its center. Outside is vacuum. Find $\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf E$ on both sides of $r=R$. Determine the bound charge on the dielectric surface and the bound charge associated with the central cavity, and verify their sum.
problems.strategy: Carry the same free-charge displacement through the dielectric boundary, changing only the constitutive conversion to electric field. Account for both the exterior material face and the source cavity before checking total bound charge.
hints: The same free charge is enclosed just inside and just outside the material boundary.
Use a different constitutive factor for E in the two regions.
Account for both the outer material surface and the inner singular-source cavity.
problems.solution: Every Gaussian sphere encloses free charge $q$, so $\mathbf D=q\hat{\mathbf r}/(4\pi r^2)$ on both sides. Inside, $\mathbf E_{\rm in}=\mathbf D/(\kappa\epsilon_0)$; outside, $\mathbf E_{\rm out}=\mathbf D/\epsilon_0$. The polarization just inside is $(1-1/\kappa)\mathbf D$. At the outer surface, $Q_{b,R}=4\pi R^2P_r=(1-1/\kappa)q$. At the central cavity, $Q_{b,0}=-(1-1/\kappa)q$. The total bound charge is zero, while the surface redistribution produces the required jump in normal E.
rubricCriteria: Obtains continuous radial D and the two piecewise electric fields.
Computes equal and opposite outer and inner bound charges.
Explains why zero total bound charge is compatible with dielectric screening.

commonErrors.description: Makes D discontinuous at an interface with no free surface sheet.
commonErrors.consequence: The normal displacement boundary law is violated.

commonErrors.description: Reports only the positive outer bound charge.
commonErrors.consequence: The compensating bound charge near the embedded free source is omitted.

problems.flawedProof: Normal electric field is the continuous boundary quantity, so both regions have $E_r=q/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^2)$. The resulting polarization has equal and opposite bound charges on the outer sphere and on a small central cavity; the constitutive change in $\mathbf D$ needs no separate free sheet.

problems.title: Susceptibility sets both polarization and permittivity
problems.objective: Convert a measured electric field into polarization, displacement, and relative permittivity with coherent SI units.
problems.statement: A linear isotropic dielectric has electric susceptibility $\chi_e=3.20$ and is placed in a uniform field $E=2.50\times10^4\,\mathrm{V/m}$. Find the polarization magnitude, displacement magnitude, and relative permittivity.
problems.strategy: Relate susceptibility to relative permittivity before evaluating polarization. Keeping the dimensionless and dimensional quantities on separate lines makes the numerical units and limiting case transparent.
hints: Relative permittivity is $1+\chi_e$, not $\chi_e$.
Multiply epsilon zero, susceptibility, and field for P.
Add the vacuum contribution before reporting D.
problems.solution: The constitutive law gives $P=\epsilon_0\chi_eE=(8.854\times10^{-12})(3.20)(2.50\times10^4)=7.08\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$. The displacement is $D=\epsilon_0E+P=\epsilon_0(1+\chi_e)E=9.30\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$. The relative permittivity is $\kappa=1+\chi_e=4.20$. Both P and D have charge-per-area units.
rubricCriteria: Computes $P=7.08\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$.
Computes $D=9.30\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$.
Reports $\kappa=4.20$ and audits units.

commonErrors.description: Sets relative permittivity equal to susceptibility.
commonErrors.consequence: The vacuum contribution is omitted from the constitutive response.

commonErrors.description: Reports polarization in volts per metre.
commonErrors.consequence: A field unit is retained instead of the dipole-moment-per-volume unit.

problems.flawedProof: Set relative permittivity equal to susceptibility, $\kappa=\chi_e=3.20$. The polarization is still $P=\epsilon_0\chi_eE=7.08\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$, and use $D=\epsilon_0\kappa E$ with that value of kappa.

problems.title: Depolarization weakens the internal field of a sphere
problems.objective: Solve the self-consistent internal field of a linear dielectric sphere using its depolarizing field.
problems.statement: A dielectric sphere with susceptibility $\chi_e$ is placed in a uniform applied field $\mathbf E_0$. A uniformly polarized sphere creates the internal depolarizing field $-\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$. Solve self-consistently for $\mathbf P$ and the total internal field. Check the limits $\chi_e\to0$ and $\chi_e\to\infty$.
permittedResults: $\mathbf E_{\rm dep}=-\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$ for a uniformly polarized sphere
problems.strategy: Insert the total internal field, including the depolarizing contribution, into the susceptibility law. Solve the resulting self-consistency equation and test both weak- and strong-response limits.
hints: Use the total internal field in the susceptibility law.
Collect all terms proportional to $\mathbf P$ on one side.
Test both weak-response and strong-response limits of the solved formula.
problems.solution: The material responds to the total internal field: $\mathbf P=\epsilon_0\chi_e(\mathbf E_0-\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0))$. Therefore $(1+\chi_e/3)\mathbf P=\epsilon_0\chi_e\mathbf E_0$, giving $\mathbf P=3\epsilon_0\chi_e\mathbf E_0/(\chi_e+3)$. The internal field is $\mathbf E_{\rm in}=\mathbf E_0-\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)=3\mathbf E_0/(\chi_e+3)$. It tends to $\mathbf E_0$ for vanishing susceptibility and to zero for very large positive susceptibility, while P approaches $3\epsilon_0\mathbf E_0$.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the correct self-consistent constitutive equation.
Derives $\mathbf P=3\epsilon_0\chi_e\mathbf E_0/(\chi_e+3)$ and $\mathbf E_{\rm in}=3\mathbf E_0/(\chi_e+3)$.
Interprets both limiting cases without calling a large-kappa dielectric automatically conducting.

commonErrors.description: Uses the applied field directly in P after introducing depolarization.
commonErrors.consequence: The induced field is counted in the output but not in the constitutive input.

commonErrors.description: Adds the depolarizing field instead of subtracting it.
commonErrors.consequence: The response becomes spuriously self-amplifying for an ordinary dielectric.

problems.flawedProof: Use the applied field directly in the constitutive law, $\mathbf P=\epsilon_0\chi_e\mathbf E_0$. The depolarizing field still subtracts, giving $\mathbf E_{\rm in}=\mathbf E_0-\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)=(1-\chi_e/3)\mathbf E_0$.

problems.title: Match a dielectric sphere to a uniform applied field
problems.objective: Determine the scalar potentials and induced dipole of a dielectric sphere by enforcing electrostatic interface conditions.
problems.statement: A sphere of radius $R$ and permittivity $\epsilon$ sits in vacuum in an applied field $E_0\hat{\mathbf z}$. Assume $V_{\rm in}=-Ar\cos\theta$ and $V_{\rm out}=-E_0r\cos\theta+B\cos\theta/r^2$. Determine $A$ and $B$, then identify the induced dipole moment.
permittedResults: Continuity of normal D when free surface charge is absent
problems.strategy: Match the two scalar potentials at the sphere first, then differentiate with the radial sign intact and impose normal displacement continuity. Read the dipole moment from the exterior inverse-square coefficient and test material-matching limits.
hints: Evaluate both potentials at $r=R$ before differentiating.
Use $E_r=-\partial V/\partial r$ with the sign intact.
Compare the coefficient of $\cos\theta/r^2$ with a point-dipole potential.
problems.solution: Continuity of potential at $r=R$ gives $A=E_0-B/R^3$. With no free surface charge, normal D is continuous: $\epsilon A=\epsilon_0(E_0+2B/R^3)$. Solving yields $A=3\epsilon_0E_0/(\epsilon+2\epsilon_0)$ and $B=R^3E_0(\epsilon-\epsilon_0)/(\epsilon+2\epsilon_0)$. Since a dipole potential is $p\cos\theta/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^2)$, the induced moment is $\mathbf p=4\pi\epsilon_0R^3(\epsilon-\epsilon_0)\mathbf E_0/(\epsilon+2\epsilon_0)$. Equal permittivities give no dipole, and large permittivity gives the conducting-sphere exterior coefficient.
rubricCriteria: Derives the two independent boundary equations.
Solves for A and B without a sign or permittivity swap.
Extracts the induced dipole and checks equal-material and large-permittivity limits.

commonErrors.description: Matches normal E instead of normal D.
commonErrors.consequence: The dielectric discontinuity is erased and the coefficients are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates the inverse-square potential term with the wrong sign.
commonErrors.consequence: The radial boundary equation and induced dipole fail the vacuum limit.

problems.flawedProof: Both components of E are continuous, so $A=E_0$ and $B=0$ for every permittivity. A homogeneous sphere therefore cannot polarize.

problems.title: A dielectric cylinder responds differently across its axis
problems.objective: Compare longitudinal and transverse depolarization for a long dielectric cylinder and expose the role of geometry.
problems.statement: An infinitely long circular dielectric cylinder has susceptibility $\chi_e$. For a uniform applied field parallel to its axis, symmetry gives no depolarizing field. For a uniform applied field perpendicular to its axis, use the supplied depolarizing field $\mathbf E_{\rm dep}=-\mathbf P/(2\epsilon_0)$. Find the internal field and polarization in both orientations.
permittedResults: $\mathbf E_{\rm dep}=-\mathbf P/(2\epsilon_0)$ for transverse polarization of an infinite circular cylinder
problems.strategy: Treat axial and transverse excitation as distinct boundary-value problems rather than as one material formula. Only the transverse case closes through a depolarizing-field self-consistency equation.
hints: Treat the axial and transverse geometries as separate boundary-value problems.
Only the transverse case needs a self-consistent induced field.
Compare the two polarizations at the same susceptibility and applied field.
problems.solution: For an axial applied field, the curved surface normal is perpendicular to P and there are no end faces, so $\mathbf E_{\rm in}=\mathbf E_0$ and $\mathbf P_{\parallel}=\epsilon_0\chi_e\mathbf E_0$. For a transverse field, self-consistency gives $\mathbf P=\epsilon_0\chi_e(\mathbf E_0-\mathbf P/(2\epsilon_0))$. Hence $\mathbf P_{\perp}=2\epsilon_0\chi_e\mathbf E_0/(\chi_e+2)$ and $\mathbf E_{{\rm in},\perp}=2\mathbf E_0/(\chi_e+2)$. The same material therefore has a shape- and orientation-dependent finite-body response.
rubricCriteria: Finds the unchanged axial internal field and polarization.
Solves the transverse self-consistency equation.
Explains why susceptibility alone does not fix the finite specimen response.

commonErrors.description: Uses the spherical depolarizing factor for the cylinder.
commonErrors.consequence: A geometry-dependent coefficient is replaced by the wrong shape.

commonErrors.description: Applies transverse depolarization to the axial orientation.
commonErrors.consequence: The absence of polarization charge in the ideal axial geometry is ignored.

problems.flawedProof: The axial field has no depolarizing correction, but for the transverse cylinder use the spherical factor $1/3$. This gives $\mathbf E_{{\rm in},\perp}=3\mathbf E_0/(\chi_e+3)$ and $\mathbf P_\perp=3\epsilon_0\chi_e\mathbf E_0/(\chi_e+3)$.

problems.title: A dielectric interface keeps E, D, and bound charge distinct
problems.objective: Adapt the held interface anchor by deriving oriented boundary laws, solving field refraction, and separating net from material-face bound charge.
problems.statement: Two linear isotropic dielectrics meet at $z=0$, with permittivities $\epsilon_1$ below and $\epsilon_2$ above. The normal $\hat{\mathbf n}=+\hat{\mathbf z}$ points from 1 to 2, and the free surface density is $\sigma_f$. Derive the electrostatic boundary conditions. For $\sigma_f=0$, an incident field in medium 1 has magnitude $E_1$ and angle $\theta_1$ from the normal. Find $E_{2n}$, $E_{2t}$, and the angle relation. Then give the net bound sheet charge and the bound charge on each material face. Check equal-permittivity and large-$\epsilon_2$ limits without identifying a dielectric limit with a conductor.
problems.strategy: Fix the interface orientation once, derive the displacement and electric boundary laws, and resolve the incident field into normal and tangential pieces. Keep each material-face polarization charge separate until the net-sheet and limiting checks.
hints: Use one declared normal for the D jump and opposite outward normals for the two material faces.
Resolve the incident field into normal and tangential components before forming the angle ratio.
Keep the free sheet explicit when relating the total E jump to net bound charge.
problems.solution: A pillbox and loop give $\epsilon_2E_{2n}-\epsilon_1E_{1n}=\sigma_f$ and $\mathbf E_{2t}=\mathbf E_{1t}$. When $\sigma_f=0$, $E_{2n}=(\epsilon_1/\epsilon_2)E_1\cos\theta_1$ and $E_{2t}=E_1\sin\theta_1$, so $\tan\theta_2=(\epsilon_2/\epsilon_1)\tan\theta_1$. The material-face charges are $\sigma_{b1}=\mathbf P_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=(\epsilon_1-\epsilon_0)E_{1n}$ and $\sigma_{b2}=\mathbf P_2\cdot(-\hat{\mathbf n})=-(\epsilon_2-\epsilon_0)E_{2n}$. Their sum is $\sigma_b=\epsilon_0(E_{2n}-E_{1n})-\sigma_f$; for zero free sheet it reduces to $\epsilon_0(E_{2n}-E_{1n})$. Equal permittivities transmit the field unchanged. As $\epsilon_2$ grows with fixed finite boundary data, its normal field tends to zero while the tangential field remains continuous; that scalar limit alone does not impose conductor equipotential conditions or free-charge rearrangement.
rubricCriteria: Derives the oriented E and D interface laws.
Obtains the transmitted components and dielectric refraction relation.
Separates both face charges from their net and states the large-permittivity limit with correct scope.

commonErrors.description: Interchanges continuity of normal D with continuity of normal E.
commonErrors.consequence: The material response and free surface source are assigned to the wrong field.

commonErrors.description: Calls the infinite-permittivity dielectric limit a conductor proof.
commonErrors.consequence: Equipotential behavior and mobile free charge are asserted without the conductor assumptions that produce them.

problems.flawedProof: Every component of both $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf D$ is continuous at a dielectric boundary. Therefore $E_{2n}=E_{1n}$, $E_{2t}=E_{1t}$, and the two polarization face charges cancel exactly for any finite permittivities.

problems.title: Inserting dielectric at fixed free charge lowers field energy
problems.objective: Compare capacitor energy before and after dielectric insertion under an explicitly isolated-charge constraint.
problems.statement: An isolated parallel-plate capacitor has plate area $A$, separation $d$, and fixed free charges $\pm Q$. It is initially vacuum and is then completely filled with a linear dielectric of relative permittivity $\kappa$. Find the initial and final fields, voltages, and stored field energies. Identify where the energy difference goes in a quasistatic insertion.
problems.strategy: Hold free charge fixed throughout the insertion, so displacement is the conserved field variable. Compare the two capacitances and fixed-charge energies, then interpret the signed energy decrease mechanically.
hints: Fixed free charge fixes D rather than voltage.
Use the changed capacitance in the fixed-Q energy expression.
Account for the lost field energy through the mechanical insertion process.
problems.solution: The fixed free charge gives $D=Q/A$ throughout. Initially $E_i=Q/(\epsilon_0A)$, $V_i=Qd/(\epsilon_0A)$, and $U_i=Q^2d/(2\epsilon_0A)$. After insertion, $E_f=Q/(\kappa\epsilon_0A)=E_i/\kappa$, $V_f=V_i/\kappa$, and $U_f=Q^2d/(2\kappa\epsilon_0A)=U_i/\kappa$. The decrease $U_i-U_f$ becomes mechanical work and, for a real dissipative insertion, possibly heat; no battery exchanges charge because the capacitor is isolated.
rubricCriteria: Finds both fields and voltages with the factor of kappa.
Finds the energy reduction by the same factor.
Explains the energy transfer without invoking battery work.

commonErrors.description: Keeps voltage fixed for an isolated capacitor.
commonErrors.consequence: The electrical constraint is silently changed and gives the wrong energy trend.

commonErrors.description: Says the missing field energy is destroyed.
commonErrors.consequence: Energy conservation is violated by omitting insertion work or dissipation.

problems.flawedProof: Electrical isolation fixes the capacitor voltage during insertion. Therefore $Q_f=\kappa Q$, $V_f=V_i$, and $U_f=\kappa U_i$; the dielectric itself supplies the added charge and field energy.

problems.title: Fixed voltage reverses the capacitor energy bookkeeping
problems.objective: Distinguish field energy, battery work, and mechanical force when a dielectric fills a voltage-clamped capacitor.
problems.statement: A parallel-plate capacitor remains connected to an ideal battery at fixed voltage $V$ while a dielectric of relative permittivity $\kappa$ fills it completely. Compare charge and field energy with their vacuum values. Compute the battery work and the mechanical work delivered to the dielectric during a quasistatic insertion.
permittedResults: $W_{\rm battery}=V\Delta Q$ for quasistatic fixed voltage
problems.strategy: Allow the voltage source to supply additional charge while the dielectric enters. Compute battery work independently of stored-field energy; their difference supplies the mechanical work and fixes the force direction.
hints: Allow charge to flow when voltage is clamped.
Compare battery work with the change in field energy rather than equating them.
The remaining energy is mechanical work by the electric field.
problems.solution: Let $C_0=\epsilon_0A/d$ and $C_f=\kappa C_0$. At fixed V, charge increases from $Q_0=C_0V$ to $Q_f=\kappa C_0V$. The field energy rises from $U_0=C_0V^2/2$ to $U_f=\kappa C_0V^2/2$, so $\Delta U=(\kappa-1)C_0V^2/2$. The battery delivers $W_{\rm bat}=V(Q_f-Q_0)=(\kappa-1)C_0V^2$. Energy conservation leaves $W_{\rm mech}=W_{\rm bat}-\Delta U=(\kappa-1)C_0V^2/2$ as positive work done by the field while pulling the dielectric in.
rubricCriteria: Computes the charge and energy increases.
Computes battery work with the correct factor of two relative to the energy change.
Obtains the positive mechanical work and interprets the inward force.

commonErrors.description: Uses the fixed-charge energy formula while holding voltage fixed.
commonErrors.consequence: The battery exchange is excluded despite being essential to the constraint.

commonErrors.description: Equates all battery work with stored field energy.
commonErrors.consequence: The mechanical attraction of the dielectric receives no energy source.

problems.flawedProof: A fixed voltage source preserves the capacitor's initial charge $Q_0$. Since $C_f=\kappa C_0$, use $U_f=Q_0^2/(2C_f)=U_0/\kappa$ and take the battery work to be zero.

problems.title: Partial insertion turns capacitance into a force law
problems.objective: Model a partly filled capacitor as parallel regions and derive its fixed-voltage pull-in force.
problems.statement: A dielectric slab of relative permittivity $\kappa$ is inserted a distance $x$ into a parallel-plate capacitor of plate length $L$, width $w$, and gap $d$. Neglect fringing and take $0<x<L$. The voltage is fixed at $V$. Find $C(x)$ and the force on the slab using electric coenergy.
problems.strategy: Partition the occupied and unoccupied plate areas into parallel capacitors sharing one voltage. Differentiate the resulting capacitance with respect to insertion depth under the fixed-voltage constraint.
hints: Split the plate area, not the plate separation.
Parallel sub-capacitors add their capacitances.
Differentiate capacitance while holding V fixed.
problems.solution: The filled and vacuum regions share the same voltage and therefore act in parallel. Their areas are $wx$ and $w(L-x)$, so $C(x)=\epsilon_0w[L+(\kappa-1)x]/d$. At fixed voltage, the mechanical force follows from coenergy as $F_x=(V^2/2)dC/dx=\epsilon_0w(\kappa-1)V^2/(2d)$. It points toward increasing x for $\kappa>1$. Within the no-fringing model it is independent of x; edge fields supply the actual localized traction.
rubricCriteria: Builds the correct parallel capacitance model.
Differentiates it to obtain the force magnitude and direction.
States the no-fringing scope and explains the constant-force idealization.

commonErrors.description: Treats the filled and unfilled areas as series layers.
commonErrors.consequence: The geometry and capacitance dependence on insertion depth are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Uses a minus derivative of field energy at fixed voltage without battery coenergy.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted force points outward despite the dielectric attraction.

problems.flawedProof: Treat the filled and vacuum plate areas as series capacitors, form the resulting decreasing $C(x)$, and then apply the correct fixed-voltage coenergy rule $F_x=(V^2/2)dC/dx$. The negative derivative predicts an outward force.

problems.title: Maxwell stress gives dielectric surface pressure
problems.objective: Use the electrostatic stress tensor to compute traction on a conductor and recover the capacitor pressure.
problems.statement: In vacuum, the electrostatic Maxwell stress is $T_{ij}=\epsilon_0(E_iE_j-\delta_{ij}E^2/2)$. A conductor surface has outward normal $\hat{\mathbf n}$ into vacuum and electric field $\mathbf E=E_n\hat{\mathbf n}$ just outside. Find the traction exerted by the field on the conductor. Apply it to a parallel-plate capacitor at fixed field magnitude E and give the attractive pressure.
problems.strategy: Contract the Maxwell tensor with the conductor's outward normal after setting the equilibrium tangential field to zero. Repeat the orientation on each plate rather than reusing one global normal.
hints: Contract the second tensor index with the surface normal.
For a conductor, the tangential electrostatic field vanishes at equilibrium.
Energy density and pressure share SI dimensions.
problems.solution: The vacuum traction on the surface is $\mathbf t=\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$. With a purely normal field, $\mathbf t=\epsilon_0(E_n^2-E_n^2/2)\hat{\mathbf n}=(\epsilon_0E_n^2/2)\hat{\mathbf n}$. Thus the field pulls the conductor outward into the vacuum region. For either plate of an ideal capacitor, the traction points toward the opposite plate and has pressure $p=\epsilon_0E^2/2$. Multiplying by area gives the force; the units are joules per cubic metre, equal to pascals.
rubricCriteria: Derives $\mathbf t=(\epsilon_0E_n^2/2)\hat{\mathbf n}$.
Applies the normal orientation to show plate attraction.
Checks pressure units and distinguishes local traction from total force.

commonErrors.description: Omits the isotropic negative half-E-squared term.
commonErrors.consequence: The pressure is overestimated by a factor of two.

commonErrors.description: Uses one global normal for both capacitor plates.
commonErrors.consequence: One traction direction is reversed and the plates appear to accelerate together.

problems.flawedProof: Drop the isotropic term and keep only $\epsilon_0E_iE_j$. This gives $\mathbf t=\epsilon_0E_n^2\hat{\mathbf n}$; using each plate's own outward normal still makes the two tractions point into the gap.

problems.title: Charging work selects the one-half factor
problems.objective: Derive linear-dielectric field energy by quasistatic charging and distinguish it from an arbitrary nonlinear constitutive law.
problems.statement: A linear dielectric region is charged quasistatically from zero field to final fields $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$. Show that the work density is $u=\int_{\mathbf0}^{\mathbf D}\mathbf E(\mathbf D')\cdot d\mathbf D'=\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D/2$. Explain why the same one-half formula cannot be assumed for a nonlinear dielectric.
permittedResults: $du=\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf D$ for reversible quasistatic charging
problems.strategy: Parameterize reversible charging by displacement and integrate the instantaneous electric field along that constitutive path. Linear response produces the half factor, while the integral form remains valid for a nonlinear law.
hints: Parameterize the charging path by the magnitude of D.
Use linear proportionality before evaluating the integral.
For a nonlinear response, compare an integral with the endpoint product.
problems.solution: Along the linear charging path, $\mathbf E(\mathbf D')=\mathbf D'/\epsilon$ and the direction is fixed. Therefore $u=\int_0^D(D'/\epsilon)\,dD'=D^2/(2\epsilon)=\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D/2=\epsilon E^2/2$. The integral is path-independent for this reversible linear constitutive law. In a nonlinear dielectric, E is not proportional to D, so the area under the constitutive curve is generally not half the final rectangle. Hysteresis would add path dependence and dissipation, outside the assumed reversible model.
rubricCriteria: Evaluates the constitutive work integral explicitly.
Obtains the equivalent forms $D^2/(2\epsilon)$, $\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D/2$, and $\epsilon E^2/2$.
States the reversible linear assumptions and the nonlinear or hysteretic limitation.

commonErrors.description: Sets the work density equal to the final product E dot D.
commonErrors.consequence: The gradual buildup is ignored and energy is doubled in the linear case.

commonErrors.description: Extends the endpoint half-product to every nonlinear material.
commonErrors.consequence: The actual constitutive integral and possible path dependence are discarded.

problems.flawedProof: Every increment is performed at the final field, so $u=\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D$. Nonlinearity changes neither this product nor the charging path.

problems.title: The Lorentz cavity field is not the macroscopic field
problems.objective: Construct the spherical-cavity local field in a cubic dielectric and keep its macroscopic and microscopic contributions separate.
problems.statement: A uniformly polarized cubic dielectric has macroscopic fields $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf P$. In the Lorentz construction, remove a small spherical region around a molecule while treating all material outside the sphere as a continuum. Show that the continuum contribution to the local field is $\mathbf E_{\rm loc}=\mathbf E+\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$. State what additional contribution has been excluded.
permittedResults: A uniformly polarized sphere has internal field $-\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$
problems.strategy: Represent removal of the Lorentz sphere by superposing an oppositely polarized continuum sphere. Add its known interior field to the macroscopic field, then state explicitly which discrete near-neighbor contribution lies outside this construction.
hints: Represent the removed material by a superposed sphere with opposite polarization.
Reverse both the polarization and the corresponding sphere field sign.
Name the discrete sources that the exterior continuum calculation omits.
problems.solution: Removing the spherical region is equivalent to superposing a sphere with polarization $-\mathbf P$ on the original continuum. A uniformly polarized sphere produces internal field $-\mathbf P_s/(3\epsilon_0)$, so the negative-polarization sphere contributes $+\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$. Adding this cavity field to the macroscopic field gives $\mathbf E_{\rm loc}=\mathbf E+\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$. The construction has not included the discrete near-neighbor field from dipoles inside the Lorentz sphere. Cubic symmetry makes that lattice contribution vanish in the ideal model, but a general crystal or disordered local environment need not do so.
rubricCriteria: Derives the cavity contribution $+\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$.
Adds it to the macroscopic field with a declared interpretation.
States the near-neighbor limitation and the cubic-symmetry qualification.

commonErrors.description: Uses the field of a positively polarized sphere for the removed region.
commonErrors.consequence: The cavity correction is assigned the depolarizing sign instead of the opposite sign.

commonErrors.description: Calls the Lorentz result an exact microscopic field in every solid.
commonErrors.consequence: Near-neighbor and lattice-anisotropy contributions are erased without justification.

problems.flawedProof: Model removal by superposing a sphere with the original positive polarization. Its depolarizing field is $-\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$, so conclude $\mathbf E_{\rm loc}=\mathbf E-\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$ while keeping the discrete near-neighbor term separate.

problems.title: Clausius-Mossotti closes a molecular self-consistency loop
problems.objective: Derive the permittivity-density relation from molecular polarizability and evaluate a dilute numerical case.
problems.statement: A cubic dielectric contains $N$ identical molecules per unit volume, each with induced dipole $\mathbf p=\alpha\mathbf E_{\rm loc}$. Use $\mathbf P=N\mathbf p$, $\mathbf E_{\rm loc}=\mathbf E+\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$, and $\mathbf P=\epsilon_0(\kappa-1)\mathbf E$ to derive the Clausius-Mossotti relation. Evaluate $\kappa$ for $N=2.00\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$ and $\alpha=1.50\times10^{-40}\,\mathrm{C\,m^2/V}$.
problems.strategy: Substitute the Lorentz local field into the molecular dipole law before eliminating polarization in favor of relative permittivity. Solve the feedback algebra symbolically and only then evaluate the dimensionless density-polarizability parameter.
hints: Insert the local field into the molecular dipole law before replacing P by kappa.
Collect the term proportional to $N\alpha\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$.
Solve $x=(\kappa-1)/(\kappa+2)$ for kappa.
problems.solution: Self-consistency gives $\mathbf P=N\alpha(\mathbf E+\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0))$. Substituting $\mathbf P=\epsilon_0(\kappa-1)\mathbf E$ and rearranging yields $(\kappa-1)/(\kappa+2)=N\alpha/(3\epsilon_0)$. Here $x=N\alpha/(3\epsilon_0)=0.113$, so $\kappa=(1+2x)/(1-x)=1.38$. The combination $N\alpha/\epsilon_0$ is dimensionless. The modest value of x is consistent with using a linear, nonresonant induced-dipole model.
rubricCriteria: Derives the exact rational relation without dropping the local-field term.
Computes the dimensionless density parameter and kappa.
Audits units and states the dilute linear-response scope.

commonErrors.description: Uses the macroscopic field as the molecular field.
commonErrors.consequence: The local-field denominator and the Clausius-Mossotti form disappear.

commonErrors.description: Adds units to the final relative permittivity.
commonErrors.consequence: The density-polarizability combination has not been dimensionally reduced.

problems.flawedProof: Use the macroscopic field directly in the molecular law, $\mathbf p=\alpha\mathbf E$. Then $\mathbf P=N\alpha\mathbf E$ and $\kappa=1+N\alpha/\epsilon_0$, a dimensionless result with no Lorentz denominator.

problems.title: The Clausius-Mossotti pole marks model failure
problems.objective: Analyze the apparent constitutive pole and identify which microscopic assumptions fail before treating it as a material prediction.
problems.statement: Let $x=N\alpha/(3\epsilon_0)$ in the Clausius-Mossotti formula $\kappa=(1+2x)/(1-x)$. Analyze the limits $x\to0$, $x\to1^-$, and $x>1$. Explain why the pole is not by itself a controlled prediction of infinite static permittivity for an ordinary molecular dielectric.
problems.strategy: Study the rational Clausius-Mossotti expression as a function of its dimensionless parameter. Compare its small-parameter expansion with the denominator zero and interpret the pole as loss of model validity, not a stable material prediction.
hints: Expand the rational expression about zero x.
Inspect the denominator and the sign on both sides of its zero.
List assumptions that cease to be small or local near the divergence.
problems.solution: For small x, expansion gives $\kappa=1+3x+O(x^2)$, which is the dilute independent-dipole result. As $x\to1^-$, the formula diverges; for every positive $x>1$, its algebraic continuation has a positive numerator and negative denominator, hence negative static kappa. Near the pole the assumed noninteracting linear polarizabilities and Lorentz continuum local field are no longer perturbative. Correlations, lattice structure, saturation, phase transitions, dispersion, and loss can dominate. Thus the pole diagnoses an instability or breakdown of the model; it does not license extrapolating the dilute formula as a complete material law.
rubricCriteria: Obtains the correct dilute expansion and pole behavior.
Interprets the algebraic continuation without claiming universal static behavior.
Identifies concrete microscopic and dissipative limitations.

commonErrors.description: Calls the pole proof that every dense dielectric becomes a perfect conductor.
commonErrors.consequence: A model singularity is confused with mobile-charge conductor physics.

commonErrors.description: Rejects the dilute expansion because the full expression can diverge.
commonErrors.consequence: A valid controlled small-x limit is discarded because of an out-of-scope extrapolation.

problems.flawedProof: At $x=1$ the material must become an ideal conductor, and for $x>1$ its static energy is automatically stable because the formula remains algebraic.

problems.title: Thermal rotation weakens permanent-dipole polarization
problems.objective: Derive the weak-field orientational polarization and check the small-parameter and numerical scales.
problems.statement: A dilute gas has number density $N$, permanent molecular dipole magnitude $p$, temperature $T$, and applied field E. In the weak-field limit, the orientational average is $\langle\cos\theta\rangle=pE/(3k_BT)$. Derive P and evaluate it for $N=2.50\times10^{25}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $p=2.00\times10^{-29}\,\mathrm{C\,m}$, $E=1.00\times10^5\,\mathrm{V/m}$, and $T=300\,\mathrm K$. Verify the weak-field condition.
problems.strategy: Turn the weak-field orientational average into polarization by multiplying by number density and dipole magnitude. Evaluate the alignment parameter separately to verify that the approximation is self-consistent.
hints: Multiply the average dipole component by number density.
Evaluate the dimensionless ratio of dipole energy to thermal energy separately.
Use the ratio, not the field magnitude alone, to validate the approximation.
problems.solution: The polarization along the field is $P=Np\langle\cos\theta\rangle=Np^2E/(3k_BT)$. Substitution gives $P=8.05\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$. The expansion parameter is $pE/(k_BT)=4.83\times10^{-4}$, which is much smaller than one, so the linear orientational average is controlled. The response decreases as inverse temperature because thermal rotation competes with alignment.
rubricCriteria: Derives the inverse-temperature polarization law.
Computes $P=8.05\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$.
Computes the small alignment parameter and validates the linear limit.

commonErrors.description: Uses Np as the fully aligned polarization in the weak-field result.
commonErrors.consequence: Thermal orientational averaging is omitted and the response is vastly overestimated.

commonErrors.description: Compares E directly with temperature.
commonErrors.consequence: Quantities with different dimensions are used to assess the approximation.

problems.flawedProof: Every permanent dipole aligns with the field, so $P=Np=5.00\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$ regardless of temperature.

problems.title: A Lorentz cavity is not a physical vacuum inclusion
problems.objective: Separate a bookkeeping cavity used for local fields from a real cavity that changes the macroscopic boundary-value problem.
problems.statement: Compare two constructions inside a polarized dielectric: a Lorentz sphere shrunk around one molecule for a local-field calculation, and a finite physical vacuum cavity of radius a. State which sources are removed in each construction, which boundary conditions apply, and why the correction $\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$ cannot simply be added everywhere for an arbitrary real cavity.
permittedResults: Electrostatic interface conditions for E and D
problems.strategy: Separate the auxiliary Lorentz construction from a cavity that remains physically empty in the final specimen. Track the boundary conditions and the omitted discrete neighborhood in each interpretation before comparing their fields.
hints: Ask whether material is physically absent after the calculation is complete.
Identify the discrete near-neighbor region in the local-field construction.
A real boundary must be solved together with the surrounding macroscopic field.
problems.solution: The Lorentz construction removes a notional continuum sphere and then restores the explicitly treated molecule and nearby discrete dipoles. Its spherical continuum surface gives the term $\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$, while lattice symmetry controls the remaining near-neighbor contribution. A physical cavity actually removes material, has a finite dielectric-vacuum interface, and must satisfy continuity of tangential E and the appropriate normal D jump with any free surface charge. Its field depends on cavity shape, external geometry, and the self-consistent macroscopic solution. The Lorentz term equals the spherical surface contribution in a uniform continuum, but it is not a universal additive prescription for finite voids or anisotropic media.
rubricCriteria: Distinguishes the source content of the two constructions.
States the physical-cavity boundary conditions and geometry dependence.
Limits the Lorentz correction to its spherical continuum role.

commonErrors.description: Treats the notional Lorentz sphere as a manufactured void.
commonErrors.consequence: A microscopic bookkeeping device is assigned macroscopic interface physics.

commonErrors.description: Adds P over three epsilon zero for every cavity shape.
commonErrors.consequence: Shape-dependent depolarization and surrounding boundary data are ignored.

problems.flawedProof: Treat the notional Lorentz sphere as a physical spherical void that remains after the calculation. Both therefore remove continuum material permanently and obey the same dielectric-vacuum boundary conditions, with no molecule or discrete neighbors restored.

problems.title: An anisotropic dielectric tilts D away from E
problems.objective: Apply a diagonal permittivity tensor and compute the distinct field and flux directions with energy density.
problems.statement: A homogeneous anisotropic dielectric has principal permittivities $\epsilon_x=2\epsilon_0$, $\epsilon_y=3\epsilon_0$, and $\epsilon_z=5\epsilon_0$. An electric field lies in the x-z plane with $E_x=E_z=1.00\times10^4\,\mathrm{V/m}$. Find $\mathbf D$, the angle each vector makes from the positive x axis, and the energy density $u=\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D/2$.
permittedResults: $u=\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D/2$ for a linear dielectric
problems.strategy: Apply the diagonal permittivity tensor component by component rather than replacing it by a scalar average. Compute the directions of electric field and displacement independently, then use their dot product for energy positivity.
hints: Multiply each field component by its own principal permittivity.
Compute the two vector angles from their separate component ratios.
Use a dot product, not magnitudes, in the energy density.
problems.solution: The tensor law gives $\mathbf D=2\epsilon_0E_x\hat{\mathbf x}+5\epsilon_0E_z\hat{\mathbf z}$. Numerically, $D_x=1.77\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$ and $D_z=4.43\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$. E is at $45.0$ degrees, while $\tan\theta_D=D_z/D_x=2.5$, so $\theta_D=68.2$ degrees. The energy density is $(E_xD_x+E_zD_z)/2=3.10\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{J/m^3}$. Positive principal permittivities make this quadratic energy positive.
rubricCriteria: Computes both displacement components with SI units.
Finds the unequal E and D angles.
Computes positive energy density and connects it to tensor definiteness.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the tensor by the arithmetic mean permittivity.
commonErrors.consequence: The directional response and vector misalignment disappear.

commonErrors.description: Uses ED over two with vector magnitudes.
commonErrors.consequence: The angle between the fields is ignored and the quadratic energy is wrong.

problems.flawedProof: Replace the tensor by the scalar average $\epsilon_{\rm av}=(2\epsilon_0+5\epsilon_0)/2$. Then $\mathbf D=\epsilon_{\rm av}\mathbf E$, both vectors make $45$ degrees, and use $u=\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D/2$.

problems.title: A graded dielectric hides bound volume charge in its profile
problems.objective: Solve a one-dimensional graded capacitor and derive its capacitance and induced bound charge density.
problems.statement: Between plates at $z=0$ and $z=d$, a linear dielectric has $\epsilon(z)=\epsilon_0(1+\alpha z/d)$ with $\alpha>0$. There is no free volume charge. For voltage magnitude V, find D, $E(z)$, capacitance per area, and the bound volume density.
problems.strategy: With no free volume charge, keep normal displacement constant while the graded permittivity makes electric field vary. Use the voltage integral to determine that constant, and differentiate polarization to expose the bound volume density.
hints: No free volume charge makes D constant, not E.
Integrate the reciprocal permittivity to impose the voltage.
Differentiate P after expressing it in terms of the constant D.
problems.solution: Free-charge Gauss law gives constant normal D. The voltage is $V=\int_0^d[D/\epsilon(z)]\,dz=Dd\ln(1+\alpha)/(\epsilon_0\alpha)$, so $D=\epsilon_0\alpha V/[d\ln(1+\alpha)]$. Thus $E(z)=D/[\epsilon_0(1+\alpha z/d)]$ and $C/A=D/V=\epsilon_0\alpha/[d\ln(1+\alpha)]$. Since $P=D-\epsilon_0E=D[1-1/(1+\alpha z/d)]$, one obtains $\rho_b=-dP/dz=-D(\alpha/d)/(1+\alpha z/d)^2$. The negative volume charge is balanced by material-surface contributions.
rubricCriteria: Solves the voltage integral and capacitance per area.
Finds the spatial electric-field profile.
Derives the signed bound volume density and notes surface compensation.

commonErrors.description: Sets E constant because the geometry is planar.
commonErrors.consequence: The graded constitutive law then creates an unaccounted free volume charge in D.

commonErrors.description: Uses minus dD over dz for bound charge.
commonErrors.consequence: The free-charge source law is substituted for the polarization divergence.

problems.flawedProof: Planar symmetry makes $E=V/d$ everywhere. Then $P(z)=[\epsilon(z)-\epsilon_0]V/d$, so $\rho_b=-dP/dz=-\epsilon_0\alpha V/d^2$ and the capacitance follows from the average permittivity.

problems.title: Anisotropic boundary data couple direction to constitutive law
problems.objective: Solve tangential-E and normal-D matching when one medium has an off-diagonal permittivity tensor.
problems.statement: Vacuum occupies $z<0$. In $z>0$, the x-z constitutive law is $\begin{pmatrix}D_x\\D_z\end{pmatrix}=\epsilon_0\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}E_x\\E_z\end{pmatrix}$. There is no free surface charge. In vacuum just below the interface, $E_{1x}=2E_0$ and $E_{1z}=E_0$. Find $E_{2x}$, $E_{2z}$, and the direction of $\mathbf D_2$.
permittedResults: Continuity of normal D without free surface charge
problems.strategy: Enforce tangential electric continuity at the plane before using the anisotropic constitutive matrix. The normal row of that matrix, together with displacement continuity, determines the remaining field component and its unexpected direction.
hints: Fix the tangential electric component before using the tensor.
Use the z row of the tensor equation for normal displacement continuity.
Evaluate the x row only after solving the transmitted electric field.
problems.solution: Tangential E continuity gives $E_{2x}=2E_0$. Normal D continuity gives $D_{2z}=D_{1z}=\epsilon_0E_0$. The tensor law then requires $\epsilon_0(E_{2x}+3E_{2z})=\epsilon_0E_0$, so $2E_0+3E_{2z}=E_0$ and $E_{2z}=-E_0/3$. The tangential displacement is $D_{2x}=\epsilon_0(4E_{2x}+E_{2z})=(23/3)\epsilon_0E_0$. Therefore $\tan\theta_D=D_{2z}/D_{2x}=3/23$, so $\theta_D=7.43^\circ$ above the positive x axis. E and D are neither parallel nor required to refract by the scalar-permittivity formula.
rubricCriteria: Computes both displacement components from the tensor.
Explains why scalar dielectric refraction is inapplicable.

commonErrors.description: Makes the normal electric field continuous.
commonErrors.consequence: The tensor-coupled displacement boundary law is not satisfied.

commonErrors.description: Uses only diagonal tensor entries.
commonErrors.consequence: The off-diagonal coupling that reverses the transmitted normal E is lost.

problems.flawedProof: Make the normal electric field continuous as well as the tangential field, so $\mathbf E_2=(2\hat{\mathbf x}+\hat{\mathbf z})E_0$. Using the full tensor then gives $\mathbf D_2=\epsilon_0(9\hat{\mathbf x}+5\hat{\mathbf z})E_0$.

problems.title: An internal free sheet splits two displacement fields
problems.objective: Solve a voltage-constrained layered capacitor containing a prescribed free charge sheet at the dielectric interface.
problems.statement: Two dielectric layers of equal thickness d lie between plates. Their permittivities are $\epsilon_1$ and $\epsilon_2$. A free sheet charge $\sigma_f$ lies at the interface, with the normal from layer 1 to layer 2. The total voltage magnitude is V and fields are normal to the layers. Find $D_1$, $D_2$, and both electric fields, taking positive field along the normal.
problems.strategy: Write the internal free-sheet jump and the total voltage as a two-equation system for the two displacements. Solve with signs intact, then inspect whether either layer field reverses under a sufficiently strong sheet source.
hints: Write one jump equation and one total-voltage equation.
Eliminate D2 before dividing by the sum of reciprocal permittivities.
Retain signs rather than replacing fields by magnitudes mid-solution.
problems.solution: The interface law is $D_2-D_1=\sigma_f$. The voltage condition is $V=d(D_1/\epsilon_1+D_2/\epsilon_2)$. Substituting $D_2=D_1+\sigma_f$ gives $D_1=[V/d-\sigma_f/\epsilon_2]/(1/\epsilon_1+1/\epsilon_2)$ and $D_2=[V/d+\sigma_f/\epsilon_1]/(1/\epsilon_1+1/\epsilon_2)$. The fields are $E_i=D_i/\epsilon_i$. Signed values may be negative if the sheet field overwhelms the plate-imposed voltage; that represents field reversal, not a negative permittivity.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the oriented jump and voltage constraints.
Solves both displacement fields algebraically.
Converts to E and interprets possible signed reversal correctly.

commonErrors.description: Forces D1 and D2 to be equal despite the free sheet.
commonErrors.consequence: The interface source is omitted from Gauss law.

commonErrors.description: Uses absolute values inside the voltage equation.
commonErrors.consequence: Field reversal solutions are destroyed and the signed boundary problem changes.

problems.flawedProof: Normal D is always continuous, so $D_1=D_2=V/[d(1/\epsilon_1+1/\epsilon_2)]$ and the free sheet has no effect.

problems.title: A laminate has arithmetic and harmonic permittivities
problems.objective: Homogenize a fine dielectric laminate in the two principal orientations and prove the ordering of its effective responses.
problems.statement: A fine laminate consists of volume fraction f of permittivity $\epsilon_1$ and fraction $1-f$ of permittivity $\epsilon_2$. Derive the effective permittivity for a macroscopic field parallel to the layers and for a field normal to the layers. Show that the normal value does not exceed the parallel value for positive permittivities.
permittedResults: Normal D continuity without free interface charge
problems.strategy: Analyze fields parallel and perpendicular to the lamination separately. Common electric field leads to an arithmetic response, whereas common displacement and accumulated voltage lead to the harmonic response.
hints: Average D when E is common along the layers.
Average the voltage drop when D is common across layers.
Put the arithmetic and harmonic expressions over a common denominator.
problems.solution: For a parallel field, tangential E is common and volume-averaged D gives $\epsilon_{\parallel}=f\epsilon_1+(1-f)\epsilon_2$. For a normal field, D is common while voltage drops add, so $1/\epsilon_{\perp}=f/\epsilon_1+(1-f)/\epsilon_2$. Their difference is $\epsilon_{\parallel}-\epsilon_{\perp}=f(1-f)(\epsilon_1-\epsilon_2)^2/[f\epsilon_2+(1-f)\epsilon_1]$, which is nonnegative. Equality holds only for a pure phase or equal permittivities.
rubricCriteria: Derives the arithmetic parallel response.
Derives the harmonic normal response.
Proves their ordering and identifies equality cases.

commonErrors.description: Uses the arithmetic mean in both orientations.
commonErrors.consequence: The series voltage drop across normal layers is ignored.

commonErrors.description: Claims the harmonic response is larger by inspection.
commonErrors.consequence: The positive square controlling the ordering is assigned the wrong sign.

problems.flawedProof: Effective permittivity is a scalar volume average in every direction, so both orientations equal $f\epsilon_1+(1-f)\epsilon_2$.

problems.title: An ideal electret slab confines its own field
problems.objective: Find the bound sheets, electric field, and displacement of an infinite permanently polarized slab with no free charge.
problems.statement: An infinite slab occupies $-d/2<z<d/2$ and carries fixed uniform polarization $\mathbf P=P_0\hat{\mathbf z}$. Vacuum lies outside and there is no free charge anywhere. Find the bound charge, E in all three regions, and D inside the electret.
permittedResults: Field of an infinite charge sheet
problems.strategy: Convert the permanent polarization into two oppositely signed bound sheets using the slab normals. Superpose their fields region by region, then combine the interior electric field with the prescribed polarization to check the displacement source law.
hints: Use the material outward normals to sign the two bound sheets.
Superpose the sheet fields separately outside and between them.
Check D against the absence of free charge.
problems.solution: The uniform interior has $\rho_b=0$. The upper face has $\sigma_b=P_0$ and the lower face has $\sigma_b=-P_0$. Two infinite opposite sheets produce zero field outside and uniform field $\mathbf E=-P_0\hat{\mathbf z}/\epsilon_0$ inside. Hence $\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P=\mathbf0$ in the slab, consistent with zero enclosed free charge. This is a prescribed-polarization electret model, not the self-consistent law of an ordinary linear dielectric.
rubricCriteria: Finds the opposite bound surface densities.
Finds zero exterior field and the signed interior field.
Obtains zero interior D and states the electret-model scope.

commonErrors.description: Adds the two sheet fields outside the slab.
commonErrors.consequence: The cancellation of equal opposite infinite sheets is missed.

commonErrors.description: Sets E to zero because D has no free source.
commonErrors.consequence: D and E are confused in a permanently polarized medium.

problems.flawedProof: Add the two oppositely charged sheet fields in each exterior region instead of canceling them. This gives $\mathbf E=+(P_0/\epsilon_0)\hat{\mathbf z}$ above, the opposite field below, and zero electric field between the sheets.

problems.title: A spherical cavity adds a uniform polarization field
problems.objective: Derive the field inside a spherical void carved from an otherwise uniformly polarized continuum.
problems.statement: An infinite dielectric is uniformly polarized with fixed $\mathbf P$. A spherical vacuum cavity is carved out without changing the polarization far away. Using superposition with a polarized sphere, find the cavity field relative to the original macroscopic field $\mathbf E_{\rm bulk}$. State the direction of the cavity-wall bound charge normal.
permittedResults: A uniformly polarized sphere has internal field $-\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$
problems.strategy: Model the removed spherical volume as an inclusion with polarization opposite to the surrounding medium. Apply the known sphere field to that inclusion and verify the physical inner-wall normal against the superposition sign.
hints: Replace removed polarization by a sphere with the opposite vector.
Apply the known interior sphere field to that opposite polarization.
For an inner boundary, the material outward normal points into the hole.
problems.solution: The removed sphere is represented by superposing polarization $-\mathbf P$ in the cavity volume. A uniformly polarized sphere with polarization $\mathbf P_s$ has internal field $-\mathbf P_s/(3\epsilon_0)$, so the superposed negative sphere contributes $+\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$. Therefore $\mathbf E_{\rm cav}=\mathbf E_{\rm bulk}+\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$. On the physical inner wall, the dielectric outward normal points into the cavity, and $\sigma_b=\mathbf P\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}_{\rm dielectric}$. This oriented wall charge produces the same uniform correction.
rubricCriteria: Constructs the negative-polarization superposition.
Obtains $\mathbf E_{\rm cav}=\mathbf E_{\rm bulk}+\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$.
States the physical cavity-wall normal and charge convention.

commonErrors.description: Superposes a sphere with positive P.
commonErrors.consequence: The removed material is added a second time and the cavity correction reverses.

commonErrors.description: Uses the radial coordinate normal as the dielectric outward normal.
commonErrors.consequence: The inner-wall charge sign is inverted.

problems.flawedProof: Carving out the sphere is equivalent to adding another sphere polarized as $\mathbf P$, so the cavity field is $\mathbf E_{\rm bulk}-\mathbf P/(3\epsilon_0)$.

problems.title: A dielectric inclusion polarizes relative to its host
problems.objective: Generalize the dielectric-sphere solution to a host medium and identify sign reversal for a low-permittivity inclusion.
problems.statement: A spherical inclusion of radius a and permittivity $\epsilon_i$ is embedded in an infinite host of permittivity $\epsilon_h$. Far away the host field is $\mathbf E_0$. Find the uniform field inside the inclusion and its dipole moment as seen in the host. Discuss $\epsilon_i=\epsilon_h$ and $\epsilon_i<\epsilon_h$.
permittedResults: Spherical harmonic boundary matching for the dipole sector
problems.strategy: Perform the sphere boundary matching with the host permittivity as the exterior reference. Extract both the uniform inclusion field and host-observed dipole, then check equal-material and low-inclusion-permittivity limits.
hints: Replace vacuum epsilon zero by host permittivity in the exterior boundary equations.
Match potential and normal D at the inclusion radius.
Use the sign of epsilon contrast to interpret the induced dipole.
problems.solution: The same spherical boundary matching with the host as reference gives $\mathbf E_i=3\epsilon_h\mathbf E_0/(\epsilon_i+2\epsilon_h)$. The exterior dipole coefficient corresponds to $\mathbf p=4\pi\epsilon_h a^3(\epsilon_i-\epsilon_h)\mathbf E_0/(\epsilon_i+2\epsilon_h)$. Equal permittivities remove both field contrast and dipole. If $\epsilon_i<\epsilon_h$, the dipole points opposite the applied field in the host description even though the inclusion field remains aligned for positive permittivities.
rubricCriteria: Derives the inclusion internal field.
Derives the host-referenced dipole moment with dimensions.
Checks zero contrast and interprets negative contrast correctly.

commonErrors.description: Uses vacuum permittivity in the host dipole prefactor.
commonErrors.consequence: The exterior Green function and dipole dimensions are referenced to the wrong medium.

commonErrors.description: Claims a low-permittivity inclusion has an antiparallel internal E.
commonErrors.consequence: Dipole contrast sign is confused with the direction of the positive-denominator internal field.

problems.flawedProof: The internal field is $3\epsilon_h\mathbf E_0/(\epsilon_i+2\epsilon_h)$, while the exterior dipole must use the universal vacuum prefactor: $\mathbf p=4\pi\epsilon_0a^3(\epsilon_i-\epsilon_h)\mathbf E_0/(\epsilon_i+2\epsilon_h)$.

problems.title: A coated sphere can be neutral to a uniform field
problems.objective: Derive the coating fraction that cancels the dipole response of a concentric core-shell inclusion.
problems.statement: A spherical core of permittivity $\epsilon_c$ and radius a is coated to outer radius b with permittivity $\epsilon_s$, then embedded in host permittivity $\epsilon_h$. Let $f=(a/b)^3$. The coated sphere has equivalent permittivity $\epsilon_* =\epsilon_s[\epsilon_c+2\epsilon_s+2f(\epsilon_c-\epsilon_s)]/[\epsilon_c+2\epsilon_s-f(\epsilon_c-\epsilon_s)]$. Find f that makes the dipole response vanish and state the feasibility conditions.
permittedResults: A spherical inclusion has zero dipole contrast when its permittivity equals the host
problems.strategy: Impose neutrality by setting the supplied coated-sphere effective permittivity equal to that of the host. Solve the resulting volume-fraction equation and reject roots that violate the geometric or positive-material domain.
hints: Set the supplied equivalent permittivity equal to the host value.
Collect every term proportional to the volume fraction on one side.
Test whether the resulting fraction lies strictly between zero and one.
problems.solution: A sphere is dipole-neutral in the host when $\epsilon_*=\epsilon_h$. Cross multiplication gives $(\epsilon_h-\epsilon_s)(\epsilon_c+2\epsilon_s)=f(\epsilon_c-\epsilon_s)(\epsilon_h+2\epsilon_s)$. Therefore $f=(\epsilon_h-\epsilon_s)(\epsilon_c+2\epsilon_s)/[(\epsilon_c-\epsilon_s)(\epsilon_h+2\epsilon_s)]$. A physical concentric coating requires $0<f<1$, positive finite permittivities, and nonzero denominator. If those inequalities fail, no radius ratio in this isotropic two-layer design cancels the dipole. Neutrality is only for the uniform-field dipole sector; it does not make the object invisible to all spatially varying fields.
rubricCriteria: Solves the neutrality equation for the exact volume fraction.
States denominator and physical-radius feasibility conditions.
Limits the cancellation claim to the uniform dipole response.

commonErrors.description: Sets the shell permittivity equal to the host and declares neutrality for any core.
commonErrors.consequence: The core still produces contrast unless the radius or material relation also cancels it.

commonErrors.description: Accepts a negative or greater-than-one volume fraction.
commonErrors.consequence: An algebraic root is mistaken for a realizable concentric geometry.

problems.flawedProof: Dipole neutrality requires only $\epsilon_s=\epsilon_h$. Therefore every core radius and core permittivity have zero uniform-field dipole contrast, and no volume-fraction equation is needed.

problems.title: A centered charge in a spherical cavity exposes screening charge
problems.objective: Solve the field and potential of a free charge at the center of a vacuum cavity in a dielectric and compute the cavity-wall bound charge.
problems.statement: A vacuum spherical cavity of radius a is surrounded by an infinite dielectric of permittivity $\epsilon$. A free point charge q sits at the center. Find E inside and outside, the bound surface density and total bound charge on the cavity wall, and the additive constant in the interior potential when $V(\infty)=0$.
problems.strategy: Use spherical free-charge flux to fix displacement on both sides of the cavity wall. Integrate the two electric fields into a continuous potential and orient the dielectric's inner normal to obtain the screening sheet.
hints: The displacement flux encloses the same free charge in both regions.
