Use the dielectric outward normal on the inner wall.
Match the two potentials at the cavity radius to determine the interior constant.
problems.solution: Spherical free-charge flux gives $D_r=q/(4\pi r^2)$ in both regions. Hence $E_{\rm in}=q/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^2)$ and $E_{\rm out}=q/(4\pi\epsilon r^2)$. The dielectric polarization at the wall is $P_r=(\epsilon-\epsilon_0)q/(4\pi\epsilon a^2)$. Its outward normal at the inner surface is $-\hat{\mathbf r}$, so $\sigma_b=-(1-\epsilon_0/\epsilon)q/(4\pi a^2)$ and $Q_b=-(1-\epsilon_0/\epsilon)q$. Outside, $V=q/(4\pi\epsilon r)$. Continuity at a gives $V_{\rm in}=q/(4\pi\epsilon_0r)+q(1/\epsilon-1/\epsilon_0)/(4\pi a)$.
rubricCriteria: Finds both radial fields from the common D flux.
Computes the negative wall density and total screening charge.
Matches the potential constant and checks the vacuum limit.

commonErrors.description: Uses the dielectric permittivity for the field inside the vacuum cavity.
commonErrors.consequence: The local constitutive region is misidentified.

commonErrors.description: Chooses the radial coordinate normal for the dielectric at its inner wall.
commonErrors.consequence: The screening charge is assigned the wrong sign.

problems.flawedProof: Use the dielectric permittivity even inside the vacuum cavity, giving $E=q/(4\pi\epsilon r^2)$ on both sides. With the dielectric's inward wall normal, the surrounding polarization still produces a negative bound surface charge.

problems.title: Voltage and energy reveal a buried free sheet
problems.objective: Solve a coupled inverse capacitor problem from electrode charge, voltage, and stored energy, then close free, bound, and total sheet-charge audits.
problems.statement: Parallel electrodes lie at $z=0$ and $z=3.00\,\mathrm{mm}$. Layer 1 occupies $0<z<1.00\,\mathrm{mm}$ with $\epsilon_1=2\epsilon_0$; layer 2 fills the remaining $2.00\,\mathrm{mm}$ with unknown positive permittivity. An unknown free sheet may lie at their interface. Fields point along $+z$. Measurements give lower-electrode free density $\sigma_0=(6.00\times10^3\,\mathrm{V/m})\epsilon_0$, voltage drop $V=7.00\,\mathrm V$, and stored energy per area $W_A=(2.90\times10^4\,\mathrm{V^2/m})\epsilon_0$. Reconstruct $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf D$ in both layers, $\epsilon_2$, and the buried free sheet. Then determine the bound charge on all four material faces and the free charge on both electrodes. Verify the voltage, energy, interface E-jump, and global free- and bound-charge balances; explain why voltage data alone would not determine $\epsilon_2$.
permittedResults: A conductor has zero electrostatic field in its bulk
problems.strategy: Use the measured lower-electrode charge to fix the first displacement and field, then spend the remaining voltage across layer 2. Subtract the known layer-1 energy from the measured total to recover the second displacement before auditing every coincident free and bound sheet with its own normal.
hints: The lower electrode fixes $D_1=\sigma_0$ and therefore $E_1=D_1/\epsilon_1$.
After voltage determines $E_2$, the layer-2 energy term is linear in the unknown $D_2$.
List the bottom and top outward normals of each dielectric separately before summing any bound charges.
problems.solution: The lower electrode gives $D_1=(6.00\times10^3\,\mathrm{V/m})\epsilon_0$ and $E_1=3.00\,\mathrm{kV/m}$, so layer 1 drops $3.00\,\mathrm V$. The remaining $4.00\,\mathrm V$ across $2.00\,\mathrm{mm}$ gives $E_2=2.00\,\mathrm{kV/m}$. Normalize the energy equation as $2W_A/\epsilon_0=(D_1/\epsilon_0)E_1d_1+(D_2/\epsilon_0)E_2d_2$. The measured value therefore gives $5.80\times10^4=1.80\times10^4+(4.00\,\mathrm V)(D_2/\epsilon_0)$ in $\mathrm{V^2/m}$ units, so $D_2=(1.00\times10^4\,\mathrm{V/m})\epsilon_0$. Hence $\epsilon_2=D_2/E_2=5\epsilon_0$ and $\sigma_f=D_2-D_1=(4.00\times10^3\,\mathrm{V/m})\epsilon_0$. Layer 1 has polarization $P_1=(3.00\times10^3\,\mathrm{V/m})\epsilon_0$, giving bound densities $-P_1$ at the lower face and $+P_1$ at the interface. Layer 2 has $P_2=(8.00\times10^3\,\mathrm{V/m})\epsilon_0$, giving $-P_2$ at the interface and $+P_2$ at the upper face. Thus the net interface bound density is $-5.00\times10^3\epsilon_0\,\mathrm{V/m}$ and its total free-plus-bound density is $-1.00\times10^3\epsilon_0\,\mathrm{V/m}=\epsilon_0(E_2-E_1)$. The upper electrode carries $-D_2$, so electrode plus buried free charge sums to $D_1+(D_2-D_1)-D_2=0$; the four bound faces also sum to zero. Reinserted fields reproduce $7.00\,\mathrm V$ and $W_A$. Voltage fixes $E_2$ but not $D_2$ or $\epsilon_2$; the independent energy measurement supplies that missing constitutive datum. If $E_2=0$, this energy inversion would be singular.
rubricCriteria: Uses charge and voltage data to find both fields, then uses energy to obtain $D_2$ and $\epsilon_2=5\epsilon_0$.
Recovers the buried free sheet and all four oriented bound-face densities plus both electrode charges.
Closes voltage, energy, local E-jump, global neutrality, and inverse-uniqueness checks.

commonErrors.description: Assumes D is continuous across the buried interface.
commonErrors.consequence: The unknown free sheet is set to zero before the energy data can reconstruct it.

commonErrors.description: Equates measured energy with the layer-2 contribution alone.
commonErrors.consequence: The known layer-1 energy is counted twice, corrupting both $D_2$ and the inferred permittivity.

problems.flawedProof: Normal displacement is continuous at the buried interface, so $D_2=D_1=6.00\times10^3\epsilon_0\,\mathrm{V/m}$ and $\sigma_f=0$. The voltage gives $E_1=3.00\,\mathrm{kV/m}$ and $E_2=2.00\,\mathrm{kV/m}$, hence $\epsilon_2=3\epsilon_0$; these values reproduce the measured energy.

problems.title: A dielectric stack design is limited by its weakest field
problems.objective: Optimize a two-material insulation stack for capacitance while enforcing separate breakdown constraints.
problems.statement: Two dielectric layers in series have total thickness $1.00\,\mathrm{mm}$. Material 1 has $\epsilon_1=2\epsilon_0$ and breakdown field $6.00\,\mathrm{MV/m}$; material 2 has $\epsilon_2=5\epsilon_0$ and breakdown field $3.00\,\mathrm{MV/m}$. Design the minimum thickness $d_1$ of material 1 that can withstand $3.00\,\mathrm{kV}$ without either layer exceeding breakdown. Explain why this choice maximizes capacitance among feasible stacks.
permittedResults: $D$ is common in series layers without free interface charge
problems.strategy: Translate each breakdown field into an allowable displacement ceiling and identify the active material constraint. Insert that ceiling into the voltage relation, solve the thickness inequality, and use capacitance monotonicity to select the boundary design.
hints: Convert each breakdown field into a maximum displacement.
Use the smaller displacement limit in the total voltage formula.
Compare how swapping thickness from high to low permittivity changes reciprocal capacitance.
problems.solution: Series layers share D. The limits are $D\le\epsilon_1E_{b1}=12\epsilon_0\,\mathrm{MV/m}$ and $D\le\epsilon_2E_{b2}=15\epsilon_0\,\mathrm{MV/m}$, so material 1 limits D. At its limiting value, the supported voltage is $V=12\times10^6[d_1/2+(0.001-d_1)/5]=2400+3.60\times10^6d_1$ in volts. Requiring $V\ge3000$ gives $d_1\ge1.67\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm m=0.167\,\mathrm{mm}$. At equality, material 1 is at breakdown while material 2 has field $2.40\,\mathrm{MV/m}$, below its limit. Because material 2 has higher permittivity, replacing it with additional material 1 increases the series reciprocal-thickness sum and lowers capacitance, so the minimum feasible $d_1$ maximizes C.
rubricCriteria: Identifies material 1 as the displacement-limiting layer.
Derives the minimum $d_1=0.167\,\mathrm{mm}$ and checks material 2.
Proves the capacitance-optimality direction under the thickness constraint.

commonErrors.description: Chooses the lower breakdown field without multiplying by permittivity.
commonErrors.consequence: The series invariant D and the actual limiting layer are misidentified.

commonErrors.description: Maximizes the thickness of the low-permittivity layer for safety.
commonErrors.consequence: A feasible but nonoptimal design is presented without the requested capacitance argument.

problems.flawedProof: Compare the two breakdown fields directly and declare material 2 limiting because $3.00<6.00$. Its field limit times the total $1.00\,\mathrm{mm}$ already supports $3.00\,\mathrm{kV}$, so take the minimum material-1 thickness to be zero.

problems.title: Bound charge data reconstruct a radial polarization
problems.objective: Invert polarization divergence in a sphere and use regularity plus surface data to remove the integration ambiguity.
problems.statement: Inside a sphere of radius R, measurements find uniform bound volume density $\rho_b=-\rho_0$, with $\rho_0>0$, and spherical symmetry. Reconstruct every radial polarization field consistent with the volume data. Impose regularity at the origin, predict the bound surface density, and verify total bound-charge neutrality.
problems.strategy: Integrate the radial polarization equation before imposing regularity, retaining the inverse-square homogeneous term. Origin behavior fixes that constant; the reconstructed surface charge then supplies a global neutrality check.
hints: Integrate the radial divergence before dividing by r squared.
Retain the integration constant until imposing origin behavior.
Use the reconstructed field at R to close the global charge balance.
problems.solution: Write $\mathbf P=P_r(r)\hat{\mathbf r}$. The equation $-r^{-2}d(r^2P_r)/dr=-\rho_0$ integrates to $r^2P_r=\rho_0r^3/3+C$, so $P_r=\rho_0r/3+C/r^2$. The singular term represents an additional pointlike source at the origin and is excluded by regularity, giving $\mathbf P=(\rho_0r/3)\hat{\mathbf r}$. The surface density is $\sigma_b=P_r(R)=\rho_0R/3$. Then $Q_{\rm vol}=-4\pi\rho_0R^3/3$ and $Q_{\rm surf}=4\pi R^2(\rho_0R/3)$ cancel. Volume divergence data alone leave C undetermined; regularity or central-source data are essential.
rubricCriteria: Finds the one-parameter radial family.
Uses regularity to eliminate the inverse-square term.
Predicts the surface density and verifies exact neutrality.

commonErrors.description: Sets the integration constant to zero without stating a condition.
commonErrors.consequence: The inverse problem's central-source ambiguity is hidden rather than resolved.

commonErrors.description: Equates surface density to the volume density.
commonErrors.consequence: Quantities with different units are confused and neutrality cannot close.

problems.flawedProof: Integration gives $P_r=\rho_0r/3+C/r^2$. Integration constants in polarization are gauge choices, so set $C=0$ immediately; then $\sigma_b=\rho_0R/3$ and the volume and surface charges cancel.

problems.title: Uniform permittivity maximizes capacitance at fixed material average
problems.objective: Prove a variational design bound for a graded planar dielectric using a reciprocal-permittivity inequality.
problems.statement: A planar capacitor of thickness d may use any positive profile $\epsilon(z)$ satisfying the material-budget constraint $d^{-1}\int_0^d\epsilon(z)\,dz=\bar\epsilon$. There is no free volume charge. Prove that its capacitance per area satisfies $C/A\le\bar\epsilon/d$, identify equality, and explain the physical role of low-permittivity bottlenecks.
permittedResults: Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for positive integrable functions
problems.strategy: Express series capacitance through the spatial average of reciprocal permittivity. Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to permittivity and its reciprocal, and read the equality condition to identify the unique maximizing profile.
hints: Express capacitance through the integral of reciprocal permittivity.
Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to square roots of epsilon and its reciprocal.
Use the equality condition, not only the numerical bound.
problems.solution: Normal D is constant, so $V=D\int_0^d dz/\epsilon(z)$ and $C/A=[\int_0^d dz/\epsilon(z)]^{-1}$. Cauchy-Schwarz gives $(\int_0^d\epsilon\,dz)(\int_0^d dz/\epsilon)\ge d^2$. With the budget, $\int_0^d dz/\epsilon\ge d/\bar\epsilon$, hence $C/A\le\bar\epsilon/d$. Equality in Cauchy-Schwarz requires $\sqrt{\epsilon}$ proportional to $1/\sqrt{\epsilon}$ almost everywhere, so epsilon is uniform. A thin low-permittivity region receives a large field at common D and contributes disproportionately to voltage, making it a series bottleneck.
rubricCriteria: Derives the reciprocal-profile capacitance functional.
Proves the sharp upper bound from the material budget.
Identifies uniform equality and interprets low-permittivity bottlenecks.

commonErrors.description: Replaces the reciprocal integral by the reciprocal of the average without proof.
commonErrors.consequence: The desired optimization conclusion is assumed at the critical step.

commonErrors.description: Claims concentrating high permittivity in a thin layer always raises capacitance.
commonErrors.consequence: The series voltage cost of the remaining low-permittivity region is ignored.

problems.flawedProof: Capacitance depends only on the arithmetic average of epsilon, so every profile exactly equals $\bar\epsilon A/d$ and there is no equality condition to check.

problems.title: Design a radial dielectric for a constant electric field
problems.objective: Invert Gauss law to synthesize a graded spherical shell and audit positivity, voltage, and boundary limitations.
problems.statement: A free charge q is centered inside a spherical dielectric shell $a<r<b$. Design a positive isotropic permittivity profile so that the electric-field magnitude in the shell is the constant $E_0$. Find the voltage drop across the shell, polarization, and bound volume density. State what must happen at the two material boundaries and why the design cannot extend regularly to $r=0$.
problems.strategy: Let Gauss law fix radial displacement from the centered free charge, then choose permittivity so its ratio to the requested constant field is correct. Differentiate the resulting polarization and inspect both boundary sheets and the unavoidable origin singularity.
hints: Gauss law determines D before the constitutive profile is chosen.
Solve epsilon from the desired ratio D over E.
Differentiate r squared times radial P and inspect the two endpoints separately.
problems.solution: Free-charge Gauss law fixes $D_r=q/(4\pi r^2)$. Requiring $E_r=E_0$ gives $\epsilon(r)=q/(4\pi E_0r^2)$, which is positive when q and the chosen outward field have the same sign. The shell voltage drop is $E_0(b-a)$. Polarization is $P_r=D_r-\epsilon_0E_0=q/(4\pi r^2)-\epsilon_0E_0$. Since $r^2P_r=q/(4\pi)-\epsilon_0E_0r^2$, $\rho_b=-r^{-2}d(r^2P_r)/dr=2\epsilon_0E_0/r$. The dielectric outward normal is $-\hat{\mathbf r}$ at $a$ and $+\hat{\mathbf r}$ at $b$, so $\sigma_b(a)=-q/(4\pi a^2)+\epsilon_0E_0$ and $\sigma_b(b)=q/(4\pi b^2)-\epsilon_0E_0$. The volume charge is $4\pi\int_a^b\rho_b r^2\,dr=4\pi\epsilon_0E_0(b^2-a^2)$, exactly canceled by the two surface totals. The required permittivity diverges as inverse square toward the origin, so a finite-core cutoff and matched boundary media are necessary; the ideal profile is not a regular all-space passive material.
rubricCriteria: Derives the inverse-square permittivity profile and voltage.
Computes P and the bound volume density with correct signs.
Identifies boundary sheets, positivity, and the singular-core limitation.

commonErrors.description: Chooses constant permittivity for constant spherical E.
commonErrors.consequence: The inverse-square displacement required by enclosed free charge is incompatible with that constitutive choice.

commonErrors.description: Extends the inverse-square profile through the origin as a regular medium.
commonErrors.consequence: The material parameter diverges and the central free-source model is not physically resolved.

problems.flawedProof: A constant target field requires a constant permittivity, so choose $\epsilon=q/(4\pi E_0a^2)$ throughout the shell. Then take the voltage drop to be $E_0(b-a)$ and use this same finite material value all the way toward a smaller inner cutoff.

problems.title: Steady current forbids local charge accumulation
problems.objective: Use charge continuity to test whether a proposed spatially varying current can be stationary.
problems.statement: In a conducting region a proposed current density is $\mathbf J=J_0(x/L)\hat{\mathbf x}$, where $J_0$ and L are positive constants. Use the continuity equation to find the local rate of charge-density change. Can this be a steady current throughout the region without an additional current component?
problems.strategy: Evaluate the divergence of the stated current field locally and insert it into charge continuity with the correct sign. The result should be interpreted as a rate of charge accumulation, not as a new steady solution.
hints: Differentiate the x component with respect to x.
Use the sign in the continuity equation before interpreting accumulation.
Steady state requires zero total divergence, not constant current density.
problems.solution: Charge continuity is $\partial\rho/\partial t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0$. Here $\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=\partial J_x/\partial x=J_0/L$, so $\partial\rho/\partial t=-J_0/L$. The proposed field causes uniform charge depletion and is not a steady current by itself. A stationary completion would need another component whose divergence is $-J_0/L$, or boundary and time-dependent charge data consistent with the accumulation.
rubricCriteria: Computes $\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=J_0/L$.
Finds $\partial_t\rho=-J_0/L$ with units.
Rejects stationarity unless a divergence-canceling contribution is supplied.

commonErrors.description: Calls the current steady because it has no explicit time dependence.
commonErrors.consequence: A time-independent J with nonzero divergence still changes charge density.

commonErrors.description: Uses a positive sign for the charge accumulation rate.
commonErrors.consequence: The continuity equation is reversed and depletion becomes creation.

problems.flawedProof: Since $\mathbf J$ contains no explicit t, it is steady. Therefore $\partial\rho/\partial t=0$, and continuity imposes no further local condition on its spatially varying x component.

problems.title: Four endpoint-angle fields assemble a rectangular loop
problems.objective: Superpose finite-segment Biot-Savart fields to obtain the center field of a noncircular closed loop and audit two geometric limits.
problems.statement: A rectangular filamentary loop lies in the $x$-$y$ plane with vertices $(\pm a,\pm b,0)$ and carries current $I$ counterclockwise as viewed from $+z$. You may use the field magnitude $\mu_0 I\ell/[2\pi\rho\sqrt{\rho^2+\ell^2}]$ at the perpendicular bisector of one segment. To keep the audit focused on orientation and superposition, the two horizontal sides together have magnitude $\mu_0Ia/[\pi b\sqrt{a^2+b^2}]$, while the two vertical sides together have magnitude $\mu_0Ib/[\pi a\sqrt{a^2+b^2}]$. Determine the direction of each pair, add them, reduce the result for a square, and identify the dominant pair when $a\gg b$.
permittedResults: Finite straight-segment field supplied in the statement
problems.strategy: Group opposite sides because each pair has a common half-length and center distance. Orient every contribution before adding magnitudes, then simplify the symmetric expression before taking the square and large-aspect-ratio limits.
hints: Use the right-hand rule at the center before adding either supplied pair magnitude.
Put the two pair contributions over a common denominator before simplifying.
Set $a=b$ for the square, then compare the two supplied terms when $a/b$ is large.
problems.solution: The horizontal pair contributes $\mu_0Ia/[\pi b\sqrt{a^2+b^2}]$ and the vertical pair contributes $\mu_0Ib/[\pi a\sqrt{a^2+b^2}]$. The right-hand rule makes both contributions point along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Therefore $\mathbf B(0)=\mu_0I\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\,\hat{\mathbf z}/(\pi ab)$. For a square, $a=b$, this becomes $\mathbf B(0)=\sqrt2\mu_0I\hat{\mathbf z}/(\pi a)$. If $a\gg b$, the horizontal sides approach two effectively infinite antiparallel wires whose center fields add, giving the leading term $\mu_0I/(\pi b)$; the vertical-pair contribution is smaller by order $b^2/a^2$.
rubricCriteria: Orients and adds the supplied horizontal- and vertical-side contributions.
Obtains $\mathbf B(0)=\mu_0I\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\hat{\mathbf z}/(\pi ab)$.
Checks both the square reduction and the correct dominant pair for $a\gg b$.

commonErrors.description: Counts only one side from each opposite pair.
commonErrors.consequence: Both contributions are underestimated by a factor of two.

commonErrors.description: Cancels fields from opposite sides because their currents are antiparallel.
commonErrors.consequence: The observation point lies on opposite sides of the two filaments, so both cross products actually share the loop normal.

problems.flawedProof: Each opposite-side pair supplies only one independent center-field contribution. Adding one horizontal and one vertical term gives $\mathbf B(0)=\mu_0I\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\,\hat{\mathbf z}/(2\pi ab)$, with the same single-pair convention in the square and long-rectangle limits.

problems.title: Helmholtz spacing cancels the axial curvature
problems.objective: Superpose two loop fields, expand about their midpoint, and choose a separation that suppresses the leading spatial nonuniformity.
problems.statement: Two identical coaxial circular loops of radius $a$ are centered at $z=\pm s/2$. Each carries current $I$ in the same sense, producing a field along $+z$ at the midpoint. Starting from the single-loop axis field $B_z(z)=\mu_0Ia^2/[2(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}]$, derive the pair field, expand it about $z=0$ through the quadratic term, and determine the separation $s$ that makes the quadratic coefficient vanish. Give the resulting midpoint field.
permittedResults: Single-loop axis field supplied in the statement
problems.strategy: Translate the supplied one-loop field to each coil center and add the two even profiles. Differentiate the common profile at half-separation and set its quadratic curvature to zero for the uniform-field design.
hints: Write the two denominators using $z-s/2$ and $z+s/2$.
Odd powers of $z$ cancel because the pair is mirror symmetric.
problems.solution: The pair field is $B_z(z)=\frac{\mu_0Ia^2}{2}\{[a^2+(z-s/2)^2]^{-3/2}+[a^2+(z+s/2)^2]^{-3/2}\}$. Put $A=a^2+s^2/4$. Since $g''(s/2)=3(s^2-a^2)A^{-7/2}$, the midpoint expansion is $B_z(z)=\mu_0Ia^2A^{-3/2}+[3\mu_0Ia^2(s^2-a^2)/(2A^{7/2})]z^2+O(z^4)$. Hence the quadratic curvature vanishes at $s=a$. At that spacing, $B_z(0)=\mu_0I a^2/(5a^2/4)^{3/2}=8\mu_0I/(5\sqrt5\,a)$. Mirror symmetry removes the linear term for every $s$; the Helmholtz choice additionally removes the quadratic term.
rubricCriteria: Writes the correctly shifted two-loop field and uses its even symmetry.
Derives the quadratic coefficient proportional to $s^2-a^2$.
Finds $s=a$ and $B_z(0)=8\mu_0I/(5\sqrt5\,a)$.

commonErrors.description: Uses the full separation s in each translated loop argument.
commonErrors.consequence: The coils are placed at $\pm s$ instead of $\pm s/2$, changing both curvature and midpoint field.

commonErrors.description: Sets only the linear Taylor coefficient to zero.
commonErrors.consequence: Mirror symmetry already cancels that coefficient for every separation, so no uniformity design condition is obtained.

problems.flawedProof: Translate the two loop fields with arguments $z-s$ and $z+s$, placing their centers at $\pm s$. The curvature condition is then $4s^2-a^2=0$, so report the stated separation as $s=a/2$.

problems.title: Closed current loops exchange equal and opposite net forces
problems.objective: Use the Biot-Savart double integral to prove reciprocal net force for arbitrary disjoint closed filamentary circuits.
problems.statement: Two disjoint closed filamentary loops $C_1$ and $C_2$ carry steady currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ in vacuum. Let $\mathbf R=\mathbf r_2-\mathbf r_1$. Starting from Biot-Savart and $d\mathbf F_2=I_2d\boldsymbol\ell_2\times\mathbf B_1$, reduce the force on loop 2 to a symmetric double integral and prove $\mathbf F_1=-\mathbf F_2$. Identify exactly where closedness of the loops is used, and explain why the result need not hold element by element.
problems.strategy: Insert loop 1's Biot-Savart field into the force integral for loop 2 and expand the nested cross product. Closure eliminates a gradient circulation; exchanging labels then reveals the sign carried by the directed separation.
hints: Use $\mathbf a\times(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)=\mathbf b(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c)-\mathbf c(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b)$.
For fixed $\mathbf r_1$, the integral $\oint_{C_2}\mathbf R\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell_2/R^3$ is a closed integral of a gradient.
On exchanging labels, $d\boldsymbol\ell_1\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell_2$ is unchanged while $\mathbf R$ reverses.
problems.solution: Substitution gives $\mathbf F_2=\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{4\pi}\oint_{C_2}\oint_{C_1}d\boldsymbol\ell_2\times(d\boldsymbol\ell_1\times\mathbf R/R^3)$. The triple product has a term $d\boldsymbol\ell_1(d\boldsymbol\ell_2\cdot\mathbf R/R^3)$ and a term $-(d\boldsymbol\ell_1\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell_2)\mathbf R/R^3$. For fixed $\mathbf r_1$, $\mathbf R/R^3=-\nabla_2(1/R)$, so the first term integrates to zero around closed $C_2$. Thus $\mathbf F_2=-\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{4\pi}\oint_{C_1}\oint_{C_2}(d\boldsymbol\ell_1\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell_2)\mathbf R/R^3$. Swapping labels sends $\mathbf R$ to $-\mathbf R$ while leaving the scalar line-element product unchanged, proving $\mathbf F_1=-\mathbf F_2$. Closure is essential when discarding the gradient circulation. Individual current elements do not form isolated conserved current systems, so their mutual magnetic forces need not be an action-reaction pair.
rubricCriteria: Expands the nested cross product and eliminates the gradient term using loop closure.
Obtains the symmetric force kernel with the correct overall sign.
Proves reciprocal net force by label exchange and distinguishes loop-level from element-level reciprocity.

commonErrors.description: Drops the gradient term without invoking a closed contour.
commonErrors.consequence: A step that fails for an open segment is treated as a pointwise algebraic cancellation.

commonErrors.description: Exchanges loop labels but keeps the directed separation vector unchanged.
commonErrors.consequence: The sign responsible for $\mathbf F_1=-\mathbf F_2$ is lost.

problems.flawedProof: Every pair of current elements exerts equal and opposite magnetic forces by Newton's third law, so integrating immediately proves $\mathbf F_1=-\mathbf F_2$ without using loop closure.

problems.title: A changing wire area changes J but not steady I
problems.objective: Reconcile current-density variation with divergence-free steady flow through a tapered conductor.
problems.statement: A slowly tapered conductor has cross-sectional area $A(z)$ and carries steady total current I along z. Under the one-dimensional approximation, $\mathbf J=I\hat{\mathbf z}/A(z)$. Explain why the ordinary derivative $dJ_z/dz$ does not by itself prove charge accumulation in the full tapered geometry. State the correct flux test and the role of side-wall current components.
problems.strategy: Test steady flow with a complete control volume spanning two cross sections, rather than differentiating a reduced axial magnitude in isolation. The sloping boundary redirects streamlines through transverse components while preserving total current.
hints: Compare total flux through two complete cross sections.
A tapered wall changes the directions of local streamlines.
Do not promote a one-dimensional magnitude model into a complete Cartesian vector field.
problems.solution: A finite control volume between two cross sections has incoming and outgoing flux both equal to I, so its net current flux is zero in steady state. The one-dimensional expression has $dJ_z/dz\ne0$ when area changes, but a real taper has slanted side boundaries and small transverse components that redirect streamlines; a Cartesian field with only the stated z component is not the complete geometry. The correct test is $\int_V\nabla\cdot\mathbf J\,dV=\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf a=I_{\rm out}-I_{\rm in}=0$. Thus J magnitude can vary while the full current remains divergence-free.
rubricCriteria: Uses equal total cross-sectional currents to establish steady flux balance.
Explains the missing transverse geometry in the reduced expression.
States the integral continuity test and avoids claiming constant J is required.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that every spatially varying J accumulates charge.
commonErrors.consequence: Divergence is confused with variation of one component along a changing coordinate tube.

commonErrors.description: Sets J constant despite changing area and fixed I.
commonErrors.consequence: The relation between current density and cross-sectional flux is violated.

problems.flawedProof: Because $d[I/A(z)]/dz$ is nonzero, every taper must accumulate charge forever; transverse current components cannot affect divergence.

problems.title: A thick coaxial return redistributes field before cancellation
problems.objective: Resolve Ampere law through two distributed conductors and separate exact exterior cancellation from magnetic energy in the dielectric gap.
problems.statement: A coaxial line has a solid inner conductor $0<r<a$ carrying total current $+I$ uniformly and a thick outer conductor $b<r<c$ carrying total return current $-I$ uniformly over its annular area. The region $a<r<b$ is nonmagnetic insulation. Find $\mathbf B(r)$ in all four radial regions, check continuity at $a$, $b$, and $c$, and compute the magnetic energy per unit length stored only in the insulating gap.
problems.strategy: Build enclosed current separately in each radial interval, using area fractions for both conductors. After matching the field at all material radii, integrate magnetic energy only over the declared insulating annulus.
hints: Inside the outer metal, the enclosed return fraction is $(r^2-b^2)/(c^2-b^2)$.
The total enclosed current must approach zero continuously as $r\to c$.
For energy per unit length, the gap volume element is $2\pi r\,dr$.
problems.solution: Cylindrical symmetry gives $\mathbf B=B_\phi\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$. Ampere law yields $B_\phi=\mu_0Ir/(2\pi a^2)$ for $r<a$ and $B_\phi=\mu_0I/(2\pi r)$ for $a<r<b$. For $b<r<c$, the enclosed current is $I[1-(r^2-b^2)/(c^2-b^2)]=I(c^2-r^2)/(c^2-b^2)$, so $B_\phi=\mu_0I(c^2-r^2)/[2\pi r(c^2-b^2)]$. For $r>c$, the net enclosed current and field vanish. The adjacent formulas agree at all three radii because there are no idealized surface-current sheets. In the insulation, $U'_B=\int_a^b[B^2/(2\mu_0)]2\pi r\,dr=\mu_0I^2\ln(b/a)/(4\pi)$.
rubricCriteria: Derives all four field branches, including the annular return-current fraction.
Verifies continuity at each conductor boundary and zero exterior field.
Obtains $U'_B=\mu_0I^2\ln(b/a)/(4\pi)$ for the insulation alone.

commonErrors.description: Treats the thick return conductor as a surface sheet at r equal to b.
commonErrors.consequence: The field is forced to jump instead of decreasing continuously across the annulus.

commonErrors.description: Includes conductor interiors when computing the requested gap energy.
commonErrors.consequence: The reported integral no longer corresponds to the declared insulating storage region.

problems.flawedProof: The return current is already fully enclosed at $r=b$, so $B$ drops discontinuously to zero there and remains zero throughout the thick outer conductor.

problems.title: A radial current profile changes the interior power of r
problems.objective: Integrate a nonuniform cylindrical current and match its interior magnetic field to the exterior result.
problems.statement: A long cylinder of radius a carries $\mathbf J=J_0(r/a)\hat{\mathbf z}$ for $r<a$ and zero outside. Find the total current and B inside and outside. Check continuity at r equal to a.
problems.strategy: Integrate the nonuniform current density with the cylindrical area factor before applying Ampere's law. The surface value must agree between the interior power law and the exterior inverse-radius branch.
hints: Include the cylindrical area factor r prime in the current integral.
Divide the enclosed current by the Ampere-circle circumference.
Use the total integrated current for the exterior field.
problems.solution: The enclosed current is $I(r)=2\pi\int_0^rJ_0(r'/a)r'\,dr'=2\pi J_0r^3/(3a)$. Thus for $r<a$, $B_\phi(2\pi r)=\mu_0I(r)$ gives $B_\phi=\mu_0J_0r^2/(3a)$. The total current is $I=2\pi J_0a^2/3$, so outside $B_\phi=\mu_0J_0a^2/(3r)$. Both expressions give $\mu_0J_0a/3$ at the surface. The quadratic near-axis behavior reflects the vanishing central current density.
rubricCriteria: Computes the enclosed and total currents.
Derives the quadratic interior and inverse-radius exterior fields.
Checks surface continuity and near-axis behavior.

commonErrors.description: Integrates J only with dr.
commonErrors.consequence: The cylindrical area Jacobian is omitted and both current and field powers are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Extends the interior current profile beyond the conductor.
commonErrors.consequence: The exterior Ampere law encloses a fictitious growing current.

problems.flawedProof: Integrate the profile only with $dr'$, obtaining $I(r)=J_0r^2/(2a)$. Use that result for the interior Ampere field, then freeze it at $r=a$ and use the resulting total current in the correct inverse-radius exterior branch.

problems.title: A sheet-current jump does not determine the mean field
problems.objective: Separate local magnetic boundary data from the global or symmetry condition that fixes a common background field.
problems.statement: An infinite sheet at $z=0$ carries $\mathbf K=K\hat{\mathbf x}$ in vacuum. Assume the fields on both sides are uniform and parallel to $\hat{\mathbf y}$, but do not initially assume reflection antisymmetry. With $\hat{\mathbf n}=+\hat{\mathbf z}$ from the lower side to the upper side, determine the most general pair $\mathbf B_+$ and $\mathbf B_-$ allowed by the surface-current boundary condition. Identify the undetermined mean field, show how source-only reflection symmetry fixes it, and give an explicit external field that changes the mean without changing the jump.
permittedResults: $\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\mathbf B_+-\mathbf B_-)=\mu_0\mathbf K$ in vacuum
problems.strategy: Parameterize the two tangential fields by their mean and difference. The oriented jump law fixes only the latter; reflection symmetry or a specified external background is needed to choose the mean.
hints: Write $B_0=(B_{+y}+B_{-y})/2$ before applying the cross product.
Because $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=-\hat{\mathbf x}$, track the sign of the jump carefully.
A uniform added field is continuous across the sheet and therefore invisible to the jump condition.
problems.solution: Let $\mathbf B_\pm=B_{\pm y}\hat{\mathbf y}$. The boundary condition gives $\hat{\mathbf z}\times[(B_{+y}-B_{-y})\hat{\mathbf y}]=\mu_0K\hat{\mathbf x}$, hence $B_{+y}-B_{-y}=-\mu_0K$. Defining $B_0=(B_{+y}+B_{-y})/2$ gives the full family $\mathbf B_+=(B_0-\mu_0K/2)\hat{\mathbf y}$ and $\mathbf B_-=(B_0+\mu_0K/2)\hat{\mathbf y}$. For the isolated source sheet, reflection symmetry requires $\mathbf B_+=-\mathbf B_-$ and therefore $B_0=0$. Superposing any uniform external field $B_0\hat{\mathbf y}$ produces another solution with exactly the same local jump, proving that boundary data alone do not select the mean.
rubricCriteria: Uses the oriented cross product to obtain $B_{+y}-B_{-y}=-\mu_0K$.
Parameterizes the complete one-parameter family by its mean field.
Distinguishes the extra reflection condition from the boundary law and supplies a continuous external-field counterexample.

commonErrors.description: Sets the mean field to zero before applying any global condition.
commonErrors.consequence: A source-only symmetry choice is misrepresented as information contained in the local boundary law.
The sign of $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf y}$ is reversed.

problems.flawedProof: The boundary law gives two separate equations, $\mathbf B_+=-\mu_0K\hat{\mathbf y}/2$ and $\mathbf B_-=+\mu_0K\hat{\mathbf y}/2$, so adding a continuous uniform field would violate the sheet current.

problems.title: An ideal toroid confines flux by symmetry
problems.objective: Use Ampere law to find toroidal field, flux, and inductance while declaring the ideal-winding approximation.
problems.statement: An ideal toroid has N tightly wound turns carrying current I, rectangular cross section of height h, inner radius a, and outer radius b. Find B in the core, the flux through one turn, and the self-inductance. State why the exterior zero-field claim is idealized.
problems.strategy: Use a concentric Ampere circle to obtain the exact inverse-radius core field. Integrate it across the rectangular section for one-turn flux, multiply by all linked turns, and isolate the idealizations behind zero leakage.
hints: Choose a circular loop concentric with the toroid.
Integrate the inverse-radius field across the rectangular core height.
Multiply one-turn flux by N before dividing by current.
problems.solution: For $a<r<b$, a circular Ampere loop encloses NI and symmetry makes B azimuthal and constant on the loop, so $B_\phi=\mu_0NI/(2\pi r)$. Ideal symmetry gives zero field in the central hole and outside. The flux per turn is $\Phi=\int_a^bB_\phi h\,dr=\mu_0NIh\ln(b/a)/(2\pi)$. Flux linkage is $N\Phi$, hence $L=\mu_0N^2h\ln(b/a)/(2\pi)$. Discrete turns, lead wires, and finite winding pitch break exact toroidal symmetry and produce leakage fields.
rubricCriteria: Derives the inverse-radius toroidal field with its region.
Computes the logarithmic flux and N-squared inductance.
States the winding and leakage assumptions behind exterior confinement.

commonErrors.description: Treats B as constant across the radial core thickness.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact logarithmic flux is replaced by an unjustified thin-toroid approximation.

commonErrors.description: Uses one-turn flux directly as total linkage.
commonErrors.consequence: The self-inductance misses a factor of N.

problems.flawedProof: Approximate the toroidal field as exactly uniform at the mean-radius value $B=\mu_0NI/[\pi(a+b)]$. Then $\Phi=Bh(b-a)$ and, retaining all flux linkages, $L=N\Phi/I$.

problems.title: Ampere law survives when symmetry fails
problems.objective: Explain why a circular Ampere loop does not determine the field of a finite wire even though the integral law remains exact.
problems.statement: A finite straight current segment lies on the z axis. A student chooses a circle centered on the segment midpoint and writes $B(2\pi R)=\mu_0I$. Diagnose the argument. State what Ampere law says for a physically closed steady-current circuit containing the segment and why the local finite-segment field still requires more information.
problems.strategy: Separate the universal circulation law from the symmetry assumptions needed to infer a pointwise field. Restore a physically closed steady circuit, identify the lost translations, and state what full-source information Biot-Savart still requires.
hints: List the translations preserved by an infinite wire and lost by a finite one.
Check whether an isolated segment can carry time-independent current without endpoints accumulating charge.
Separate knowing a loop integral from knowing the integrand pointwise.
problems.solution: The finite segment lacks translation symmetry along z, so B need not have constant magnitude on a coaxial circle away from the special midpoint geometry, and end connections contribute to the field. More fundamentally, an isolated open steady-current segment violates charge continuity; a physical circuit must close. Ampere law remains $\oint\mathbf B\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=\mu_0I_{\rm enc}$ for a steady closed current, but the integral gives one circulation number, not the pointwise field unless symmetry fixes direction and constancy. Biot-Savart applied to the complete circuit, or an equivalent boundary-value solution, supplies the missing distribution.
rubricCriteria: Identifies the missing symmetry behind pulling B outside the integral.
Requires a physically closed steady-current circuit.
Explains why Ampere law remains true but insufficient for local field extraction.

commonErrors.description: Claims Ampere law is false for finite currents.
commonErrors.consequence: A failure of algebraic field extraction is confused with failure of Maxwell's equation.

commonErrors.description: Treats an open segment as a complete stationary source.
commonErrors.consequence: Charge conservation and return-current contributions are ignored.

problems.flawedProof: Add a physical return path so the current is steady, but declare the magnetostatic Ampere integral itself valid only for infinite-wire symmetry. Therefore the closed finite circuit is said not to obey $\oint\mathbf B\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=\mu_0I_{\rm enc}$.

problems.title: Two uniform-field potentials differ by one global gauge
problems.objective: Verify gauge equivalence of symmetric and Landau vector potentials and compare their loop circulation.
problems.statement: For uniform $\mathbf B=B_0\hat{\mathbf z}$, compare $\mathbf A_S=(B_0/2)(-y\hat{\mathbf x}+x\hat{\mathbf y})$ and $\mathbf A_L=B_0x\hat{\mathbf y}$. Verify their curls, find a single-valued scalar chi with $\mathbf A_L-\mathbf A_S=\nabla\chi$, and compute the counterclockwise circulation around a rectangle of sides a and b.
problems.strategy: Compute both curls directly, then integrate the component equations for their difference to construct a scalar gauge function. Closed-loop circulation provides an independent confirmation that the two potentials encode the same field.
hints: Take both curls component by component.
Integrate the x and y components of the potential difference to find chi.
Use the oriented magnetic flux as an independent circulation check.
problems.solution: Both curls equal $B_0\hat{\mathbf z}$. Their difference is $(B_0/2)(y\hat{\mathbf x}+x\hat{\mathbf y})=\nabla(B_0xy/2)$, so $\chi=B_0xy/2$ is a global gauge function on ordinary space. Stokes' theorem gives $\oint\mathbf A\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=B_0ab$ for either potential and counterclockwise orientation viewed from positive z. The gauges distribute the edge contributions differently, but a closed-loop gradient integral vanishes. Chi has magnetic-flux units, consistent with its gradient having vector-potential units.
rubricCriteria: Verifies both vector potentials produce the same B.
Finds $\chi=B_0xy/2$.
Obtains circulation $B_0ab$ and checks gauge and units.

commonErrors.description: Uses the negative of the required gauge function.
commonErrors.consequence: Its gradient maps the potentials in the opposite direction from the stated difference.

commonErrors.description: Claims the two loop circulations differ because their edge terms differ.
commonErrors.consequence: The integral of a globally single-valued gradient around a closed loop is not zeroed.

problems.flawedProof: Both curls and both counterclockwise rectangle circulations equal the same uniform-field values. Their difference is generated by $\chi=-B_0xy/2$, so $\mathbf A_L-\mathbf A_S=\nabla\chi$.

problems.title: Coulomb gauge turns magnetostatics into a vector Poisson problem
problems.objective: Derive the vector-potential equation, state its residual gauge freedom, and identify the boundary data needed for uniqueness.
problems.statement:
In magnetostatics take $\mathbf B=
abla	imes\mathbf A$ and impose Coulomb gauge $
abla\cdot\mathbf A=0$. Starting from $
abla	imes\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J$, derive the equation for A. Describe the residual gauge transformations and the decay or boundary conditions needed to select a solution.
problems.strategy: Expand the curl of the curl before imposing Coulomb gauge, which converts the field equation into a vector Poisson problem. Examine a subsequent gradient addition to identify the residual harmonic gauge freedom and its boundary dependence.
hints: Expand curl curl A before imposing the gauge condition.
Apply divergence to a gradient gauge addition.
Distinguish a local gauge equation from global boundary and topology data.
problems.solution:
Using $

problems.title: A decaying azimuthal field hides a return-current annulus
problems.objective: Invert an axisymmetric magnetic field to reconstruct its signed current distribution and total current.
problems.statement: An axisymmetric field is measured as $\mathbf B=B_0r e^{-r^2/a^2}\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$ for all r. Use magnetostatic Ampere law in differential form to reconstruct J. Find where the current changes sign and compute the total current through the plane.
permittedResults: Ampere law for a circular loop
problems.strategy: Invert the azimuthal field with the cylindrical curl formula for axial current density. Differentiating the product $rB_\phi$ exposes the sign-changing return region, after which an area integral checks the total current.
hints: For this symmetry, use $J_z=(\mu_0r)^{-1}d(rB_\phi)/dr$.
Factor the derivative to identify its zero and sign change.
Use the large-radius Ampere circulation to determine net current.
problems.solution: For an azimuthal field independent of z, $J_z=(1/\mu_0r)d(rB_\phi)/dr$. Since $rB_\phi=B_0r^2e^{-r^2/a^2}$, one gets $\mathbf J=(2B_0/\mu_0)e^{-r^2/a^2}(1-r^2/a^2)\hat{\mathbf z}$. It changes sign at $r=a$: the positive core is surrounded by a negative return-current region. The total enclosed current at radius r is $I(r)=2\pi rB_\phi/\mu_0=2\pi B_0r^2e^{-r^2/a^2}/\mu_0$, which tends to zero at infinity. Thus the net current is zero even though local current and magnetic field are nonzero.
rubricCriteria: Differentiates the measured field to obtain J with correct factors.
Locates and interprets the return-current annulus.
Computes zero net current from both circulation and asymptotics.

commonErrors.description: Uses dB phi over dr without the cylindrical r factor.
commonErrors.consequence: The reconstructed current misses geometric divergence and has the wrong zero.

commonErrors.description: Integrates only the positive core and calls it total current.
commonErrors.consequence: The distributed negative return current is omitted despite the decaying exterior circulation.

problems.flawedProof: Use $J_z=(1/\mu_0)dB_\phi/dr$, omitting the cylindrical factor. This gives $J_z=(B_0/\mu_0)e^{-r^2/a^2}(1-2r^2/a^2)$; integrating that expression over the full plane gives a nonzero net current.

problems.title: Gauge equivalence stops at a topological obstruction
problems.objective: Adapt the held gauge anchor by combining explicit uniform-field gauges with a curl-free but non-exact flux-tube potential.
problems.statement: First use the two uniform-field potentials $\mathbf A_S=(B_0/2)(-y\hat{\mathbf x}+x\hat{\mathbf y})$ and $\mathbf A_L=B_0x\hat{\mathbf y}$. Verify their gauge function and their circulation around a rectangle. Then remove the z axis from space and consider $\mathbf A_\Phi=\Phi\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}/(2\pi r)$ outside an ideal flux tube. Show that its curl vanishes on the punctured domain but its circulation around a linking circle is nonzero. Decide whether a global single-valued scalar gauge removes it, and state the full time-dependent gauge transformation of scalar and vector potentials.
permittedResults: Stokes theorem on surfaces contained in the domain
problems.strategy: Handle the uniform-field potentials on the simply connected plane by explicitly integrating their difference. For the excluded flux tube, test the same claim on a linking circle, where a nonzero period blocks every single-valued gauge.
hints: For the uniform pair, compute the potential difference before guessing chi.
For the flux tube, integrate A around a circle at any positive radius.
A global gradient must have zero circulation on every closed loop in its domain.
problems.solution:
The uniform potentials both have curl $B_0\hat{\mathbf z}$ and satisfy $\mathbf A_L-\mathbf A_S=
abla(B_0xy/2)$. Their counterclockwise rectangle circulation is $B_0ab$. For the flux-tube potential, the cylindrical curl vanishes wherever $r>0$, but a circle linking the removed axis has $\oint\mathbf A_\Phi\cdot d oldsymbol\ell=\Phi$. If $\mathbf A_\Phi=
abla\chi$ for a global single-valued chi, every closed-loop integral would vanish, so no such gauge exists. Locally one may write $\chi=\Phi\phi/(2\pi)$, but it changes by Phi after one turn and is multivalued. The general gauge rule is $\mathbf A'=\mathbf A+
abla\chi$ and $\varphi'=\varphi-\partial_t\chi$, leaving $\mathbf B$ and $\mathbf E=-
abla\varphi-\partial_t\mathbf A$ unchanged. Stokes cannot use a spanning disk that crosses the excluded flux tube.
rubricCriteria: Verifies the uniform gauges, global chi, and rectangle circulation.
Shows curl-free but nonzero linking circulation on the punctured domain.
Rejects a global scalar gauge, states the time-dependent rule, and respects Stokes-domain scope.

commonErrors.description: Uses curl zero as sufficient proof of a global gradient.
commonErrors.consequence: The multiply connected domain and nonzero linking circulation are ignored.

commonErrors.description: Uses the wrong sign in the scalar-potential gauge rule.
commonErrors.consequence: The transformed electric field changes and the claimed equivalence fails.

problems.flawedProof: Since $\nabla\times\mathbf A_\Phi=0$ outside the tube, $\mathbf A_\Phi=\nabla[\Phi\phi/(2\pi)]$ globally and its nonzero circulation can be removed by a single-valued gauge.

problems.title: An ideal solenoid leaves vector potential outside its field
problems.objective: Construct a continuous vector potential for an ideal solenoid and interpret its exterior circulation without erasing topology.
problems.statement: An infinite ideal solenoid of radius R has uniform field $B_0\hat{\mathbf z}$ inside and zero field outside. Seek $\mathbf A=A_\phi(r)\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$ that is regular at the axis and continuous at R. Find A inside and outside, and compute the circulation around a circle with $r>R$.
problems.strategy: Solve the cylindrical curl relation for the azimuthal potential inside and outside separately. Axis regularity removes the interior singular mode, while continuity and linked-flux circulation fix the exterior coefficient.
hints: Integrate the cylindrical curl equation separately in the two radial regions.
Remove the inverse-radius integration constant inside by axis regularity.
Use continuity at R and then compare exterior circulation with interior flux.
problems.solution: For an azimuthal potential, $B_z=r^{-1}d(rA_\phi)/dr$. Regularity gives $A_\phi=B_0r/2$ inside. Outside, zero curl gives $rA_\phi=C$; continuity at R fixes $C=B_0R^2/2$. Thus $A_\phi=B_0R^2/(2r)$ outside. A circle beyond the solenoid has circulation $2\pi rA_\phi=\pi R^2B_0$, equal to the enclosed flux. Although the local exterior curl is zero, the exterior domain around an impenetrable ideal solenoid is multiply connected, so this circulation prevents gauging A to zero globally there.
rubricCriteria: Derives the regular interior potential.
Derives the continuous inverse-radius exterior potential.
Matches circulation to flux and explains the global topological obstruction.

commonErrors.description: Sets the exterior potential to zero because exterior B is zero.
commonErrors.consequence: Continuity and nonzero linked flux are lost.

commonErrors.description: Keeps an inverse-radius term inside the axis.
commonErrors.consequence: The potential becomes singular where the physical field is regular.

problems.flawedProof: Zero exterior B forces $\mathbf A=0$ outside. Continuity then forces A and B to vanish inside as well, so the solenoid cannot carry flux.

problems.title: A planar loop's moment is its oriented area
problems.objective: Derive the area-vector form of magnetic dipole moment for an arbitrary planar filament and apply it in a tilted geometry.
problems.statement: A steady current $I$ follows an arbitrary simple closed planar curve $C$ with oriented unit normal $\hat{\mathbf n}$. Starting from $\mathbf m=(I/2)\oint_C\mathbf r\times d\boldsymbol\ell$, prove $\mathbf m=IA\hat{\mathbf n}$ without assuming a circular shape. Then apply the result to an elliptical loop of semiaxes $a$ and $b$ whose current orientation gives $\hat{\mathbf n}=(\hat{\mathbf x}+\hat{\mathbf z})/\sqrt2$. In a uniform field $\mathbf B=B_0\hat{\mathbf z}$, find the torque and dipole energy.
problems.strategy: Test the line integral against an arbitrary constant vector and convert the resulting scalar circulation with Stokes theorem. Once the area identity is established, use the ellipse's tilted normal in separate torque and energy products.
hints: For constant $\mathbf c$, rewrite $\mathbf c\cdot(\mathbf r\times d\boldsymbol\ell)$ as $(\mathbf c\times\mathbf r)\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell$.
Evaluate $\nabla\times(\mathbf c\times\mathbf r)$ before applying Stokes theorem.
The ellipse has area $\pi ab$, and only the $x$ component of its normal contributes to the torque about $y$.
problems.solution: For any constant $\mathbf c$, $\mathbf c\cdot\oint_C\mathbf r\times d\boldsymbol\ell=\oint_C(\mathbf c\times\mathbf r)\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell$. Stokes theorem and $\nabla\times(\mathbf c\times\mathbf r)=2\mathbf c$ give $2A\,\mathbf c\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$. Since this holds for every $\mathbf c$, $\oint_C\mathbf r\times d\boldsymbol\ell=2A\hat{\mathbf n}$ and therefore $\mathbf m=IA\hat{\mathbf n}$. For the ellipse, $\mathbf m=I\pi ab(\hat{\mathbf x}+\hat{\mathbf z})/\sqrt2$. Hence $\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf m\times\mathbf B=-I\pi abB_0\hat{\mathbf y}/\sqrt2$ and $U=-I\pi abB_0/\sqrt2$. The torque reduces the angle between the moment and the field, consistent with decreasing energy.
rubricCriteria: Proves the vector area identity by testing against an arbitrary constant vector and using Stokes theorem.
Obtains the correctly oriented elliptical moment.
Computes the negative-y torque and negative energy with a consistent alignment interpretation.

commonErrors.description: Claims the circular result extends by shape intuition alone.
commonErrors.consequence: The required shape-independent line-integral proof and orientation control are missing.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf x}$ for the torque.
commonErrors.consequence: The order in $\mathbf m\times\mathbf B$ is reversed, flipping the y direction.

problems.flawedProof: Visual analogy with a circular loop proves $\mathbf m=IA\hat{\mathbf n}$ for every planar curve. With $A=\pi ab$, this identity directly gives the ellipse torque and energy.

problems.title: The loop-axis field expands into a dipole plus corrections
problems.objective: Extract the far-field series of a circular loop and identify the first finite-size correction.
problems.statement: The exact axis field of a circular loop is $B_z=\mu_0Ia^2/[2(z^2+a^2)^{3/2}]$ for positive z. Expand it through relative order $a^2/z^2$ for $z\gg a$, express the leading term using $m=I\pi a^2$, and state the sign of the correction.
problems.strategy: Factor the dominant power of axial distance from the exact loop field and apply the binomial series through the first size correction. Replace current times area by magnetic moment and retain the correction sign.
hints: Factor the large z scale before expanding.
Use exponent $-3/2$ in the binomial coefficient.
Replace I times a squared by m over pi only after the expansion.
problems.solution: Factor $z^3$ from the denominator: $B_z=\mu_0Ia^2(1+a^2/z^2)^{-3/2}/(2z^3)$. The binomial expansion is $(1+x)^{-3/2}=1-3x/2+O(x^2)$. Hence $B_z=\mu_0m[1-3a^2/(2z^2)+O(a^4/z^4)]/(2\pi z^3)$. The leading term is the axial magnetic-dipole field. The first finite-loop correction is negative because spreading the source away from the origin increases every source-to-axis distance relative to the point-dipole idealization.
rubricCriteria: Performs the large-distance factorization and expansion.
Expresses the leading dipole coefficient correctly.
Gives the negative relative correction and its order.

commonErrors.description: Expands with exponent positive three halves.
commonErrors.consequence: The correction sign and coefficient are reversed.

commonErrors.description: Calls the correction another inverse-cube dipole term.
commonErrors.consequence: The extra inverse-square relative factor and finite-size order are lost.

problems.flawedProof: The denominator expansion is $1+3a^2/(2z^2)$, so a finite loop always has a larger far field than its point dipole with the same m.

problems.title: Opposite loops cancel the dipole but not the field
problems.objective: Show how a separated anti-Helmholtz pair produces a magnetic quadrupole-scale far field.
problems.statement: Two small coaxial loops centered at $z=+s/2$ and $z=-s/2$ have moments $+m\hat{\mathbf z}$ and $-m\hat{\mathbf z}$. For observation points on the positive axis with $z\gg s$, use the dipole-axis field to find the leading combined field and its distance scaling.
permittedResults: Axis field of a point magnetic dipole
problems.strategy: Write the signed, shifted dipole fields of the two opposing loops before expanding in separation over observation distance. Their leading dipoles cancel, leaving the first derivative term and its faster decay.
hints: Write the two signed dipole fields using their shifted axial distances.
Expand both inverse cubes to first order in s over z.
Confirm that the inverse-cube terms cancel before interpreting the remainder.
problems.solution: The upper positive loop contributes $C/(z-s/2)^3$ and the lower negative loop contributes $-C/(z+s/2)^3$, where $C=\mu_0m/(2\pi)$. Expanding to first order in s over z gives $(z-s/2)^{-3}-(z+s/2)^{-3}=3s/z^4+O(s^3/z^6)$. Therefore $B_z=3\mu_0ms/(2\pi z^4)+O(z^{-6})$. The net magnetic dipole moment is zero, but separation leaves a quadrupole-type moment with inverse-fourth-power axial decay. Reversing both currents reverses the field; setting s to zero cancels it.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the signed shifted dipole fields.
Derives $B_z=3\mu_0ms/(2\pi z^4)$ at leading order.
Interprets zero net dipole, inverse-fourth decay, and limiting signs.

commonErrors.description: Adds the two dipole moments despite opposite currents.
commonErrors.consequence: A spurious inverse-cube far field survives.

commonErrors.description: Cancels the entire field because the net dipole is zero.
commonErrors.consequence: Higher multipole structure from source separation is discarded.

problems.flawedProof: Ignore the opposite orientation and add the two loop moments as $m_{\rm net}=2m$. The far-axis field is then $B_z=\mu_0m/(\pi z^3)$ at leading order, with no cancellation of the inverse-cube term.

problems.title: Magnetic scalar potential needs a current-free simple domain
problems.objective: Derive the scalar-potential equation for H and exhibit its global failure around a linked free current.
problems.statement: In a linear homogeneous region with no free current, explain when one may write $\mathbf H=-\nabla\psi_m$ and what equation psi satisfies. Then consider the region outside an infinite straight free current I with the current axis removed. Decide whether one global single-valued magnetic scalar potential exists there.
permittedResults: Poincare lemma on simply connected domains
problems.strategy: Distinguish a locally curl-free magnetic field from a globally exact one by testing loop periods. Where a scalar potential exists, combine it with zero magnetic divergence to obtain its boundary-value equation.
hints: Separate local curl-free behavior from global exactness.
Use divergence B after introducing the scalar potential.
Evaluate H circulation around a loop that links the excluded current.
problems.solution:
Where $
abla	imes\mathbf H=\mathbf J_f=0$, a simply connected domain admits $\mathbf H=-
abla\psi_m$. If the permeability is constant and $
abla\cdot\mathbf B=0$, then $
abla^2\psi_m=0$. Outside the line current, local curl H is zero, but a circle linking the removed axis has $\oint\mathbf H\cdot d oldsymbol\ell=I$. A global single-valued gradient would have zero circulation, so no such scalar exists on the full punctured domain. Locally one can use a potential proportional to the azimuthal angle, but it is multivalued after one circuit.
rubricCriteria: States the current-free and simply connected conditions.
Derives the Laplace equation in a homogeneous region.
Uses nonzero linked-current circulation to prove global failure.

commonErrors.consequence: The punctured topology and linked-current circulation are ignored.

commonErrors.description: Uses divergence H equals zero in every magnetic medium.
commonErrors.consequence: Magnetization and permeability variation are silently excluded from the source equation.

problems.flawedProof: Because curl H vanishes outside the wire, a global single-valued scalar always exists and its circulation can equal I around a closed loop.

problems.title: A localized steady current has origin-independent dipole moment
problems.objective: Prove the translation invariance of magnetic dipole moment using steady-current localization rather than assuming it.
problems.statement: For a localized steady current, define $\mathbf m=(1/2)\int\mathbf r\times\mathbf J\,d^3r$. Shift the coordinate origin by constant vector a, so $\mathbf r'=\mathbf r-\mathbf a$. Prove that m is unchanged. Justify the identity $\int\mathbf J\,d^3r=\mathbf0$ from continuity and localization.
problems.strategy: Translate the moment integral and isolate the origin-dependent term as a constant vector crossed with total current density. Prove that integral vanishes componentwise using steady continuity, localization, and the divergence theorem.
hints: Expand the translated moment and isolate the integral of J.
Apply divergence theorem to $x_i\mathbf J$ component by component.
Use both zero divergence and decay of the boundary flux.
problems.solution: Under the shift, $\mathbf m'=(1/2)\int(\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\times\mathbf J\,d^3r=\mathbf m-(1/2)\mathbf a\times\int\mathbf J\,d^3r$. For component i, integrate $\partial_j(x_iJ_j)=J_i+x_i\partial_jJ_j$. Steady continuity gives $\partial_jJ_j=0$, and localization makes the surface integral of $x_i\mathbf J$ vanish at infinity. Hence $\int J_i\,d^3r=0$ for every component, so $\mathbf m'=\mathbf m$. If current crosses the boundary or is not localized, the discarded surface term can be nonzero and the proof does not apply.
rubricCriteria: Computes the exact translation correction to m.
Proves $\int\mathbf J\,d^3r=0$ from a surface identity.
States localization and boundary limitations of the result.

commonErrors.description: Declares the integral of J zero only because current is a vector.
commonErrors.consequence: The essential continuity and boundary proof is missing.

commonErrors.description: Drops the translation term without checking boundary current.
commonErrors.consequence: Origin invariance is asserted for open or nonlocalized systems where it need not follow.

problems.flawedProof: The integral $\int\mathbf J\,d^3r$ vanishes automatically because positive and negative vector components cancel in an all-space integral. This vector-cancellation rule alone makes the translation term zero.

problems.title: Uniform magnetization is an ideal solenoidal surface current
problems.objective: Convert a uniformly magnetized infinite cylinder into bound currents and recover its H and B fields.
problems.statement: An infinite cylinder of radius R has uniform magnetization $\mathbf M=M_0\hat{\mathbf z}$ and no free current. Find the bound volume and surface currents. Use their solenoid analogy to find H and B inside and outside.
permittedResults: Field of an ideal infinite solenoid
problems.strategy: Evaluate volume curl and boundary cross product of the uniform magnetization independently. Interpreting the surviving azimuthal surface current as a solenoid winding then yields the interior and exterior fields.
hints: Take curl M in the volume before evaluating its boundary cross product.
Compare the azimuthal surface current with turns per length times current.
Use B equals mu zero times H plus M only inside matter.
problems.solution: Uniform M has $\mathbf J_b=\nabla\times\mathbf M=\mathbf0$. At the curved surface, $\mathbf K_b=\mathbf M\times\hat{\mathbf r}=M_0\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$; there are no end faces for the infinite cylinder. This is the surface current of an ideal infinite solenoid, so $\mathbf B_{\rm in}=\mu_0M_0\hat{\mathbf z}$ and $\mathbf B_{\rm out}=\mathbf0$. Since there is no free current, Ampere law for H and the infinite-cylinder demagnetizing factor give $\mathbf H=\mathbf0$ in both regions. Inside, $\mathbf B=\mu_0(\mathbf H+\mathbf M)$; outside M is zero.
rubricCriteria: Finds zero volume and azimuthal surface bound current.
Obtains the confined axial B field.
Separates zero H from nonzero B and states the infinite-cylinder idealization.

commonErrors.description: Sets B to zero because no free current is present.
commonErrors.consequence: Magnetization bound current and the M term in B are omitted.

commonErrors.description: Uses K equal to normal cross M.
commonErrors.consequence: The surface current direction reverses and conflicts with the solenoid field.

problems.flawedProof: The bound currents are $\mathbf J_b=0$ and $\mathbf K_b=\mathbf M\times\hat{\mathbf r}=M_0\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$. Nevertheless, because the free current is zero, set both $\mathbf H$ and $\mathbf B$ to zero everywhere.

problems.title: A magnetized sphere carries its own demagnetizing field
problems.objective: Find the internal H and B of a uniformly magnetized sphere and match its exterior dipole moment.
problems.statement: A sphere of radius R has prescribed uniform magnetization $\mathbf M=M_0\hat{\mathbf z}$ and no free current. Use the spherical demagnetizing factor $1/3$ to find H and B inside. Find its magnetic dipole moment and describe the exterior field.
permittedResults: $\mathbf H_{\rm demag}=-\mathbf M/3$ for a uniformly magnetized sphere
problems.strategy: Apply the sphere's demagnetizing factor to magnetic field intensity, not directly to induction. Add magnetization when converting to induction, and compare the resulting moment with the uniformly magnetized volume.
hints: Apply the supplied demagnetizing factor to H, not directly to B.
Add M when converting internal H to B.
Integrate uniform magnetization over the sphere volume.
problems.solution: The demagnetizing field of a uniformly magnetized sphere is $\mathbf H_{\rm in}=-\mathbf M/3$. Therefore $\mathbf B_{\rm in}=\mu_0(\mathbf H+\mathbf M)=2\mu_0\mathbf M/3$. The total magnetic moment is $\mathbf m=\int\mathbf M\,dV=(4\pi R^3/3)M_0\hat{\mathbf z}$. Outside the sphere, M vanishes and the field is exactly the dipole field of this moment for the uniform-sphere solution. The nonzero H is produced by the finite body's pole-equivalent boundary data even though free current is absent.
rubricCriteria: Finds $\mathbf H_{\rm in}=-\mathbf M/3$.
Finds $\mathbf B_{\rm in}=2\mu_0\mathbf M/3$.
Computes the dipole moment and identifies the exterior dipole field.
