commonErrors.consequence: The constitutive M contribution is left out after finding H.

commonErrors.description: Uses sphere surface area in the magnetic moment.
commonErrors.consequence: Magnetization per volume is integrated with the wrong measure.

problems.flawedProof: Apply the demagnetizing factor directly to induction and write $\mathbf B_{\rm in}=-\mu_0\mathbf M/3$. Separately integrate the uniform magnetization over volume to obtain $\mathbf m=(4\pi R^3/3)M_0\hat{\mathbf z}$.

problems.title: H follows free current while B follows the medium
problems.objective: Solve a current-carrying coaxial region filled with magnetic material and separate free from bound response.
problems.statement: A long free line current I runs along positive z through a homogeneous linear magnetic medium of permeability mu. Find H, B, and M for $r>0$. If $\mu=\mu_0(1+\chi_m)$, state which field is fixed by the free current independent of susceptibility.
problems.strategy: Determine magnetic field intensity from enclosed free current before invoking the medium law. Only afterward multiply by permeability for induction, which keeps free and bound source roles distinct.
hints: Use free current in the circulation law for H.
Apply the constitutive factor only after H is known.
Express M from B equals mu zero times H plus M.
problems.solution: Cylindrical symmetry and Ampere law for H give $\mathbf H=I\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}/(2\pi r)$ because the enclosed free current is I. The constitutive law gives $\mathbf B=\mu I\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}/(2\pi r)$ and $\mathbf M=\chi_m I\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}/(2\pi r)$. Thus H is set directly by free current in this homogeneous geometry, while B and M scale with the material response. If material boundaries are introduced, bound currents and boundary conditions must be included; the all-space homogeneous result cannot simply be pasted across them.
rubricCriteria: Derives the azimuthal H field from free current.
Converts to B and M with correct factors.
States the homogeneous-medium and boundary limitation.

commonErrors.description: Uses total bound plus free current in Ampere law for H.
commonErrors.consequence: The purpose of H as a free-current source field is defeated.

commonErrors.description: Makes H proportional to permeability.
commonErrors.consequence: The material factor is applied twice and the free-current circulation changes.

problems.flawedProof: Use total free plus bound current in the circulation law for $\mathbf H$: $\oint\mathbf H\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=I_f+I_b$. Thus material bound current changes $\mathbf H$ even before the constitutive conversion to $\mathbf B$.

problems.title: A hysteresis loop is not a single constitutive function
problems.objective: Diagnose when the shorthand B of H fails and identify the extra state information required in ferromagnetic media.
problems.statement: A solver models a ferromagnetic core by a single-valued curve $\mathbf B=\mathbf B(\mathbf H)$ and computes the same B whenever H returns to a prior value. Explain why this can fail under cyclic drive. Distinguish differential permeability, remanence, coercivity, and hysteretic loss, and state when a single-valued approximation is defensible.
permittedResults: Work per volume over a magnetic cycle is represented by the appropriate constitutive loop integral
problems.strategy: Treat magnetization as a history-dependent branch variable rather than a function of instantaneous field alone. Locate remanence and coercivity on the loop, then connect its oriented area with dissipated energy per cycle.
hints: Ask whether material state is determined by instantaneous H alone.
Define each named quantity relative to a branch or complete cycle.
Separate a calibrated small-signal approximation from a universal material law.
problems.solution: A ferromagnet can retain domain-state memory, so B depends on the drive history as well as the instantaneous H. Differential permeability is the local slope along a specified branch, not a global ratio. Remanence is nonzero B after H returns to zero, coercivity is the reverse H needed to bring B or M through zero under a declared convention, and the loop area is energy dissipated per volume per cycle. A single-valued law is defensible for a specified reversible minor-signal regime, an anhysteretic model, or a path restricted to one calibrated branch. It cannot predict branch switching or loss without internal state variables and evolution rules.
rubricCriteria: Explains constitutive memory and failure of a single-valued global curve.
Correctly distinguishes slope, intercept, reversal scale, and loop loss.
States controlled regimes where a single-valued approximation is acceptable.

commonErrors.description: Calls differential permeability B divided by H everywhere.
commonErrors.consequence: A local branch slope is confused with a secant ratio and history dependence disappears.

commonErrors.description: Treats remanence as free current remaining in the coil.
commonErrors.consequence: Material magnetization memory is assigned to the external circuit source.

problems.flawedProof: A hysteresis branch has differential permeability $B/H$ at each point. Remanence, coercivity, and loop area can then be read from the same branch using this secant material parameter.

problems.title: A magnetization gradient is a bound volume current
problems.objective: Compute the distributed bound current of a radially graded axial magnetization and audit its surface term.
problems.statement: An infinite cylinder of radius a has $\mathbf M=M_0(1-r^2/a^2)\hat{\mathbf z}$ inside and zero outside. Find the bound volume current and bound surface current on the curved boundary. Explain the direction and why the surface term vanishes despite a discontinuity in derivative.
problems.strategy: Take the cylindrical curl of the radial magnetization profile with explicit orientation. Evaluate the material surface current from the limiting magnetization itself and use integrated current to check the distributional boundary term.
hints: Use the cylindrical curl component generated by a radial derivative of M z.
Evaluate M itself, not its derivative, at the material boundary.
Check the azimuthal sign from the cross-product basis orientation.
problems.solution: For an axial function of r, $(\nabla\times\mathbf M)_\phi=-dM_z/dr$. Here $dM_z/dr=-2M_0r/a^2$, so $\mathbf J_b=(2M_0r/a^2)\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$. At the curved surface, $\mathbf K_b=\mathbf M(a)\times\hat{\mathbf r}=\mathbf0$ because M itself tapers to zero at r equal to a. A derivative jump changes the volume-current profile but does not create a delta-function surface current unless M has a finite tangential jump. The positive-azimuthal current direction follows z cross r.
rubricCriteria: Derives the radial-linear azimuthal volume current.
Finds zero curved-surface current from the tapered endpoint.
Explains why a derivative jump alone is not a surface-current sheet.

commonErrors.description: Uses positive dM z over dr for the phi curl.
commonErrors.consequence: The bound-current circulation direction is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Creates a surface current from the nonzero interior derivative.
commonErrors.consequence: The boundary law depends on the tangential value jump of M, not its slope alone.

problems.flawedProof: The azimuthal curl component is $J_{b,\phi}=dM_z/dr=-2M_0r/a^2$. Since $M(a)=0$, the surface-current law gives $\mathbf K_b=0$.

problems.title: Magnetic interfaces conserve normal B and jump tangential H
problems.objective: Derive the oriented magnetic boundary conditions and apply them with a free surface current.
problems.statement: Media 1 and 2 meet with normal $\hat{\mathbf n}$ from 1 to 2 and free surface current $\mathbf K_f$. Derive the boundary laws for normal B and tangential H. For $\hat{\mathbf n}=\hat{\mathbf z}$ and $\mathbf K_f=K\hat{\mathbf x}$, determine the required jump in the y component of H.
problems.strategy: Use a pillbox to conserve normal induction and a narrow loop to obtain the tangential intensity jump. Resolve the cross product in the declared normal order before translating between fields in the two media.
hints: Use a pillbox for the normal component and a loop for the tangential one.
Keep the declared normal order in H2 minus H1.
Evaluate z cross y before solving the scalar jump.
problems.solution: A magnetic pillbox and $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0$ give $(\mathbf B_2-\mathbf B_1)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=0$. A narrow loop and $\nabla\times\mathbf H=\mathbf J_f$ give $\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\mathbf H_2-\mathbf H_1)=\mathbf K_f$. With normal z and K along x, $\hat{\mathbf z}\times[(H_{2y}-H_{1y})\hat{\mathbf y}]=-(H_{2y}-H_{1y})\hat{\mathbf x}=K\hat{\mathbf x}$, so $H_{2y}-H_{1y}=-K$. Tangential B need not obey the same jump when permeabilities differ.
rubricCriteria: Derives both interface laws from Maxwell equations.
Finds $H_{2y}-H_{1y}=-K$.
States why tangential B can differ in dissimilar media.

commonErrors.description: Makes normal H continuous instead of normal B.
commonErrors.consequence: The divergence-free magnetic flux law is assigned to the wrong auxiliary field.

commonErrors.description: Drops the cross-product sign for the y-component jump.
commonErrors.consequence: The inferred sheet-current direction reverses.

problems.flawedProof: Assign the divergence law to $\mathbf H$ and set $(\mathbf H_2-\mathbf H_1)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=0$. The oriented loop law is otherwise used correctly, giving $H_{2y}-H_{1y}=-K$.

problems.title: An ellipsoid solves magnetization by one self-consistent factor
problems.objective: Derive the internal response of a linear ellipsoid and compare sphere, needle, and plate limits.
problems.statement: A linear magnetic ellipsoid is placed in uniform applied field $\mathbf H_0$ along a principal axis with demagnetizing factor N. Assume uniform magnetization $\mathbf M=\chi_m\mathbf H_{\rm in}$ and $\mathbf H_{\rm in}=\mathbf H_0-N\mathbf M$. Solve for H inside, M, and B. Discuss N equal to zero, one third, and one.
permittedResults: $\mathbf H_{\rm demag}=-N\mathbf M$ along a principal axis
problems.strategy: Insert the demagnetizing field into the constitutive response to form one scalar self-consistency equation along the principal axis. Solve for internal field, magnetization, and induction, then examine shape and high-susceptibility limits.
hints: Insert the internal field, not applied field, into the constitutive law.
Collect the product N times susceptibility before solving.
Interpret the three N values as distinct specimen geometries.
problems.solution: Substitution gives $(1+N\chi_m)\mathbf H_{\rm in}=\mathbf H_0$, so $\mathbf H_{\rm in}=\mathbf H_0/(1+N\chi_m)$ and $\mathbf M=\chi_m\mathbf H_0/(1+N\chi_m)$. The induction is $\mathbf B=\mu_0(1+\chi_m)\mathbf H_0/(1+N\chi_m)$. A long needle magnetized along its axis has N near zero and little demagnetization. A sphere has $N=1/3$. A thin plate magnetized normal to its face has N near one and the strongest suppression of internal H for positive susceptibility. Shape therefore enters even with the same intrinsic chi.
rubricCriteria: Solves the self-consistent H and M fields.
Converts them to B without dropping M.
Correctly orders the demagnetizing strength of needle, sphere, and plate.

commonErrors.description: Uses M equals chi times applied H directly.
commonErrors.consequence: The finite-body self-field is omitted from the constitutive input.

commonErrors.description: Calls N a material constant.
commonErrors.consequence: Geometry dependence is misassigned to intrinsic susceptibility.

problems.flawedProof: Magnetization is always $\chi_m\mathbf H_0$ independent of shape, so N changes neither internal H nor B.

problems.title: A spherical magnetic cavity reverses the inclusion construction
problems.objective: Find the field correction of a spherical void in a uniformly magnetized medium and distinguish H from B inside the cavity.
problems.statement: An infinite medium has prescribed uniform magnetization M and macroscopic field $\mathbf H_{\rm bulk}$. A spherical vacuum cavity is carved out. Use superposition with a sphere magnetized as negative M to find H and B in the cavity relative to the bulk fields.
permittedResults: A uniformly magnetized sphere has internal $\mathbf H=-\mathbf M/3$
problems.strategy: Represent the spherical cavity by superposing an oppositely magnetized sphere on the original medium. Convert its demagnetizing intensity into the cavity correction and audit both normal induction and tangential intensity at the wall.
hints: Represent removed magnetization by an inclusion with the opposite M.
Apply the sphere's demagnetizing H to that negative inclusion.
Inside vacuum, convert H to B without adding the removed M.
problems.solution: Removing the material is equivalent to adding a sphere with magnetization $-\mathbf M$. A uniformly magnetized sphere has internal demagnetizing field $-\mathbf M_s/3$, so the added sphere contributes $+\mathbf M/3$ to H. Therefore $\mathbf H_{\rm cav}=\mathbf H_{\rm bulk}+\mathbf M/3$. In the vacuum cavity, magnetization is zero, so $\mathbf B_{\rm cav}=\mu_0\mathbf H_{\rm cav}$. By contrast, the original bulk induction was $\mu_0(\mathbf H_{\rm bulk}+\mathbf M)$. The cavity correction depends on spherical shape and uniform background assumptions.
rubricCriteria: Builds the negative-magnetization superposition.
Finds $\mathbf H_{\rm cav}=\mathbf H_{\rm bulk}+\mathbf M/3$.
Computes cavity B and distinguishes it from the original bulk induction.

commonErrors.description: Adds negative M over three to the cavity H.
commonErrors.consequence: The sign of the removed-sphere superposition is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Uses B equals mu zero times H plus the original M inside vacuum.
commonErrors.consequence: The magnetization that was physically removed is counted in the cavity constitutive law.

problems.flawedProof: Represent removal by a sphere with the original positive magnetization, giving $\mathbf H_{\rm cav}=\mathbf H_{\rm bulk}-\mathbf M/3$. Since the cavity is vacuum, still use $\mathbf B_{\rm cav}=\mu_0\mathbf H_{\rm cav}$.

problems.title: A permeability interface rotates B around a free current sheet
problems.objective: Solve full vector boundary data at a magnetic interface with dissimilar permeabilities and a directed free surface current.
problems.statement: Medium 1 below $z=0$ has permeability $\mu_1$ and medium 2 above has $\mu_2$. The normal is positive z and a free sheet current $\mathbf K_f=K\hat{\mathbf x}$ lies at the interface. Just below, $\mathbf B_1=B_x\hat{\mathbf x}+B_y\hat{\mathbf y}+B_z\hat{\mathbf z}$. Find all components of $\mathbf B_2$.
permittedResults: Tangential H jump by free surface current
problems.strategy: Preserve normal induction across the interface before resolving the free-current jump in tangential intensity. Solve the component equations in field-intensity variables, then convert each side with its own permeability.
hints: Preserve B z directly before working on tangential components.
Expand z cross the unknown H difference in x and y components.
Convert H back to B with the permeability on each side.
problems.solution: Normal B continuity gives $B_{2z}=B_z$. The H jump satisfies $\hat{\mathbf z}\times(\mathbf H_2-\mathbf H_1)=K\hat{\mathbf x}$. Writing the tangential difference as $\Delta H_x\hat{\mathbf x}+\Delta H_y\hat{\mathbf y}$ gives $\Delta H_x\hat{\mathbf y}-\Delta H_y\hat{\mathbf x}=K\hat{\mathbf x}$. Hence $\Delta H_x=0$ and $\Delta H_y=-K$. Therefore $B_{2x}=\mu_2B_x/\mu_1$ and $B_{2y}=\mu_2(B_y/\mu_1-K)$, while $B_{2z}=B_z$. The current sheet changes only the H component perpendicular to K within the interface.
rubricCriteria: Keeps the normal induction continuous.
Solves both tangential H component jumps with correct signs.
Converts to the three B2 components and interprets the current direction.

commonErrors.description: Makes every B component continuous.
commonErrors.consequence: The permeability contrast and free-current H jump are both lost.

commonErrors.description: Places the K jump in H x.
commonErrors.consequence: The interface cross product is not evaluated and the response rotates incorrectly.

problems.flawedProof: Make every component of $\mathbf B$ continuous across the permeability interface, so $\mathbf B_2=\mathbf B_1$. The free sheet current is then treated as having no effect on the magnetic boundary data.

problems.title: Magnetic gap pressure equals its field energy density
problems.objective: Derive the attraction between high-permeability pole faces from vacuum Maxwell stress and state the leakage assumptions.
problems.statement: Two broad high-permeability pole faces are separated by a narrow vacuum gap containing approximately uniform normal field $\mathbf B=B_g\hat{\mathbf n}$. Neglect fringing. Use the vacuum magnetic stress tensor $T_{ij}=(B_iB_j-\delta_{ij}B^2/2)/\mu_0$ to find the traction and attractive pressure on a pole face. Evaluate it for $B_g=0.800\,\mathrm T$.
permittedResults: The supplied vacuum magnetic stress tensor
problems.strategy: Evaluate Maxwell traction on the two sides of a pole gap with the normal aligned to the field. The dyadic and isotropic terms combine into the energy-density pressure, whose direction follows from the opposing face normals.
hints: Use a field parallel to the chosen surface normal.
Keep both the dyadic and isotropic half-B-squared terms.
Convert tesla-squared over mu zero to pascals.
problems.solution: Contracting T with the normal gives $\mathbf t=\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=(B_g^2/2\mu_0)\hat{\mathbf n}$ for a purely normal field. Each pole face is pulled into the gap, so the attractive pressure is $p=B_g^2/(2\mu_0)$. At $0.800\,\mathrm T$, $p=2.55\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$. This equals the vacuum magnetic energy density. Finite pole permeability, fringing, saturation, and nonuniform gap fields require integrating the local stress rather than multiplying one value by area.
rubricCriteria: Derives $p=B_g^2/(2\mu_0)$.
Computes $2.55\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$.
States direction and the nonuniform, leakage, and saturation limitations.

commonErrors.description: Omits the isotropic stress term and doubles pressure.
commonErrors.consequence: The tensor contraction is incomplete.

commonErrors.description: Applies the uniform-gap value over a strongly fringing geometry without qualification.
commonErrors.consequence: A local approximation is promoted to an exact total force.

problems.flawedProof: Magnetic pressure is $B_g^2/\mu_0$ because only the dyadic term matters, and it pushes the pole faces out of the gap.

problems.title: Positive magnetic energy bounds mutual inductance
problems.objective: Derive the positivity constraint on a two-coil inductance matrix and identify the perfect-coupling equality case.
problems.statement: Two reciprocal linear coils have flux-linkage matrix $\begin{pmatrix}L_1&M\\M&L_2\end{pmatrix}$ and energy $W=(L_1I_1^2+2MI_1I_2+L_2I_2^2)/2$. Prove the necessary and sufficient conditions for nonnegative energy for all currents. Interpret equality in the determinant condition.
permittedResults: Positive-semidefinite criterion for a symmetric two-by-two matrix
problems.strategy: View stored magnetic energy as a quadratic form in the two independent currents. Completing a square, or testing its determinant, gives the exact mutual-inductance bound and the equality case.
hints: Treat energy as a quadratic form in the two currents.
Complete one square and inspect the remaining coefficient.
Translate determinant equality into a zero-energy eigen-combination.
problems.solution: The quadratic form is nonnegative for every current vector exactly when the symmetric inductance matrix is positive semidefinite. Thus $L_1\ge0$, $L_2\ge0$, and $L_1L_2-M^2\ge0$. Equivalently, complete the square: $2W=L_1(I_1+MI_2/L_1)^2+(L_2-M^2/L_1)I_2^2$ when $L_1>0$. Hence $|M|\le\sqrt{L_1L_2}$. Equality makes one eigenvalue zero and corresponds to ideal perfect coupling: one signed current combination produces no independent leakage-flux energy. Real separated coils normally satisfy strict inequality.
rubricCriteria: Derives the diagonal and determinant positivity conditions.
Obtains $|M|\le\sqrt{L_1L_2}$.
Interprets equality as ideal perfect coupling rather than negative energy.

commonErrors.description: Requires M itself to be nonnegative.
commonErrors.consequence: Winding orientation can change the sign of M without changing energy positivity.

commonErrors.description: Allows the magnitude of M to exceed the geometric mean.
commonErrors.consequence: A current combination then gives negative stored magnetic energy in a passive linear system.

problems.flawedProof: Require the inductance matrix to have nonnegative diagonal entries and determinant, but also impose $M\ge0$. This gives the orientation-dependent restriction $0\le M\le\sqrt{L_1L_2}$.

problems.title: Neumann reciprocity makes mutual inductance symmetric
problems.objective: Prove mutual-inductance reciprocity by exchanging two closed filamentary loops in the double integral.
problems.statement: For two disjoint closed filamentary circuits, use the Neumann expression $M_{12}=\mu_0(4\pi)^{-1}\oint_{C_1}\oint_{C_2}d\boldsymbol\ell_1\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell_2/|\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2|$ to prove $M_{12}=M_{21}$. State the assumptions and explain how orientation affects the sign without breaking reciprocity.
permittedResults: Exchange of convergent integrals for disjoint loops
problems.strategy: Write each mutual inductance as the same Neumann double integral with source and receiver labels exchanged. Track loop orientations and state the linear reciprocal-medium assumptions needed for the symmetry argument.
hints: Exchange both source labels in the distance kernel.
Use symmetry of the line-element dot product.
Track what happens when one closed-loop orientation is reversed.
problems.solution: The kernel is symmetric because $|\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2|=|\mathbf r_2-\mathbf r_1|$, and the dot product is symmetric under exchange of the line elements. Interchanging the order and labels of the two closed integrals therefore gives exactly the Neumann expression for $M_{21}$. Reversing one circuit orientation reverses the corresponding line element and hence both definitions of the mutual coefficient under the same terminal convention. Reciprocity assumes the same linear reciprocal medium, quasistatic coupling, and fixed geometry; nonreciprocal media or active time-varying systems need not satisfy this simple scalar relation.
rubricCriteria: Proves equality by explicit exchange of the double integral.
Handles orientation and mutual-inductance sign consistently.
States linear, reciprocal, quasistatic, and disjoint-geometry assumptions.

commonErrors.description: Claims reciprocity forces M positive.
commonErrors.consequence: Equality under label exchange is confused with an orientation-dependent sign convention.

commonErrors.description: Applies the proof unchanged to an active nonreciprocal medium.
commonErrors.consequence: The symmetric Green-function kernel assumed by the Neumann expression is no longer justified.

problems.flawedProof: The symmetric Neumann kernel proves $M_{12}=M_{21}$, and because every distance in the kernel is positive, conclude that M itself must be positive. Keep the proof restricted to the supplied passive reciprocal setting.

problems.title: Virtual work changes sign when the source constraint changes
problems.objective: Derive electromechanical force from inductance at fixed current and reconcile it with fixed-flux energy.
problems.statement: A one-coil actuator has inductance $L(x)$ that increases with insertion coordinate x. Derive the quasistatic force at fixed current I using magnetic coenergy. Then hold flux linkage lambda fixed instead and derive the force from stored energy. Show that the physical direction agrees when the correct independent variable is used.
permittedResults: Force from the appropriate energy or coenergy derivative
problems.strategy: Use magnetic coenergy when current is the controlled source variable and ordinary energy when flux linkage is controlled. Differentiate the appropriate potential at fixed control variable and reconcile the apparently opposite algebraic signs.
hints: Choose current as the independent variable for coenergy.
Choose flux linkage as the independent variable for ordinary stored energy.
Substitute lambda equals LI only after taking the specified derivative.
problems.solution: For a linear coil, coenergy at fixed current is $W'(I,x)=L(x)I^2/2$, so $F_x=(\partial W'/\partial x)_I=I^2L'(x)/2$, toward larger inductance. At fixed flux linkage, the stored energy is $W(\lambda,x)=\lambda^2/[2L(x)]$. With no source work, $F_x=-(\partial W/\partial x)_\lambda=\lambda^2L'(x)/[2L(x)^2]$. Since $I=\lambda/L$, this is again $I^2L'(x)/2$. Using minus the fixed-current field-energy derivative without including source work would predict the wrong sign.
rubricCriteria: Derives the fixed-current coenergy force.
Derives the fixed-flux energy force with the correct minus sign.
Shows equality and explains the source-work sign trap.

commonErrors.description: Uses minus dW over dx at fixed current without source work.
commonErrors.consequence: The actuator is predicted to move toward lower inductance.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates after replacing fixed lambda by L times a fixed I.
commonErrors.consequence: The independent-variable constraint is changed mid-derivative.

problems.flawedProof: At fixed current, $F=-I^2L'(x)/2$, while at fixed flux the force is positive, so the same actuator reverses merely by how it is described.

problems.title: Inductance eigenmodes expose the lowest-energy current ratio
problems.objective: Diagonalize a coupled-coil energy form, optimize it under a current-norm constraint, and interpret signed mutual coupling without confusing a negative cross term with negative energy.
problems.statement: Two reciprocal coils have $L_1=4.00\,\mathrm{mH}$, $L_2=9.00\,\mathrm{mH}$, and $M=3.00\,\mathrm{mH}$ under a stated dot convention. Find the coupling coefficient and the two eigenvalues of the inductance matrix. Subject to $I_1^2+I_2^2=5.00\,\mathrm{A^2}$, determine the current ratios and stored energies of the minimum- and maximum-energy modes. Then evaluate the energy at $(I_1,I_2)=(2.00,-1.00)\,\mathrm A$ and compare it with the true minimum. Explain what changes, and what does not, if the reference direction of coil 2 is reversed.
permittedResults: Rayleigh-quotient extremum for a symmetric matrix
problems.strategy: Diagonalize the symmetric inductance matrix before imposing the current constraint. Its normalized eigenvectors give the extremizing ratios; the specified opposing-current pair can then be compared with the lower mode, while a terminal reversal is treated as a simultaneous coordinate and mutual-sign change.
hints: The eigenvalues solve $(L_1-\lambda)(L_2-\lambda)-M^2=0$.
For either eigenvalue, use $I_2/I_1=(\lambda-L_1)/M$ before normalizing.
Reversing coil 2 changes both $I_2$ and signed M in the coordinate description.
problems.solution: The coupling coefficient is $k=3.00/\sqrt{(4.00)(9.00)}=0.500$. The inductance eigenvalues are $\lambda_\pm=(13\pm\sqrt{61})/2\,\mathrm{mH}$, numerically $2.595\,\mathrm{mH}$ and $10.405\,\mathrm{mH}$. Their current ratios are $I_2/I_1=(\lambda_\pm-4.00\,\mathrm{mH})/(3.00\,\mathrm{mH})$, namely $-0.468$ for the low-energy mode and $2.135$ for the high-energy mode. On $I_1^2+I_2^2=5.00\,\mathrm{A^2}$, the extrema are $W_{\min}=5\lambda_-/2=6.49\,\mathrm{mJ}$ and $W_{\max}=5\lambda_+/2=26.0\,\mathrm{mJ}$. At $(2,-1)\,\mathrm A$, $W=8.00-6.00+4.50=6.50\,\mathrm{mJ}$, slightly above the exact minimum because ratio $-0.500$ is not the eigenvector ratio. Reversing coil-2 reference sends $I_2\mapsto-I_2$ and $M\mapsto-M$; the matrix changes by an orthogonal sign conjugation, but eigenvalues, physical fields, and energy extrema do not.
rubricCriteria: Computes $k=0.500$ and both exact inductance eigenvalues.
Finds and normalizes the two extremizing current ratios under the stated constraint.
Compares the specified current pair with the true minimum and proves dot-reference invariance.

commonErrors.description: Extremizes the mutual term while ignoring both self-energy terms.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed current ratio is not an eigenmode of the full quadratic form.

commonErrors.description: Reverses the coil-2 current coordinate without reversing signed M.
commonErrors.consequence: A change of dot convention is mistaken for a physical change in stored energy.

problems.flawedProof: Minimize only the mutual term and choose $I_2=-I_1$ under the norm constraint, independently of the unequal self-inductances. A coil-2 reference reversal still changes both signed M and the coordinate $I_2$, so physical energy remains invariant.

problems.title: A solenoid plunger is pulled toward larger overlap
problems.objective: Derive a constant-force ideal magnetic actuator from overlap-dependent inductance and connect it to gap stress.
problems.statement: An ideal high-permeability plunger enters a long coil. Over a working range, its inductance is modeled as $L(x)=L_0+\alpha x$ with $\alpha>0$, and current I is held fixed. Find force and source-energy partition for a quasistatic displacement dx. Explain how this agrees with magnetic pressure pulling high-permeability material into a strong-field region.
problems.strategy: Differentiate the overlap-dependent inductance at fixed current to obtain the mechanical force. Balance source work, changing field energy, and motion so the direction toward larger overlap is not inferred from Lenz's law alone.
hints: Differentiate the linear inductance with current held fixed.
Compare source work with the change in one-half L I squared.
Relate the sign of dL over dx to reluctance reduction.
problems.solution: Fixed-current coenergy gives $F_x=(1/2)I^2dL/dx=\alpha I^2/2$, constant and directed toward increasing overlap. The field energy changes by $dW=(1/2)I^2dL=F_x\,dx$. The source changes flux linkage by $d\lambda=I\,dL$, so it supplies $I\,d\lambda=I^2dL=2F_x\,dx$. Half becomes increased field energy and half becomes mechanical work. The direction matches Maxwell-stress intuition: replacing a high-reluctance gap region by high-permeability material raises L and the field pulls the plunger inward. Saturation, leakage, and end fringing make real L nonlinear in x.
rubricCriteria: Derives $F_x=\alpha I^2/2$ and its inward direction.
Computes the two-to-one source work and its equal field/mechanical split.
Connects inductance gradient to stress and states real-device limitations.

commonErrors.description: Uses force equal to I squared times dL over dx.
commonErrors.consequence: The coenergy one-half factor is omitted and mechanical work is doubled.

commonErrors.description: Says all source work becomes mechanical work.
commonErrors.consequence: The simultaneous increase in stored field energy is ignored.

problems.flawedProof: Magnetic energy and coenergy are both $LI^2$. Therefore $F_x=\alpha I^2$ toward increasing overlap, and source work $2I^2dL$ splits equally into field-energy increase $I^2dL$ and mechanical work $I^2dL$.

problems.title: A field jump fixes current but not magnetic loading
problems.objective: Invert two-sided magnetic data for a surface current, reconcile Lorentz and stress-tensor loads, and expose the common-mode null space of the local inverse problem.
problems.statement: In vacuum, a planar sheet at $z=0$ has measured fields $\mathbf B_+=B_+\hat{\mathbf x}+B_n\hat{\mathbf z}$ above and $\mathbf B_-=B_-\hat{\mathbf x}+B_n\hat{\mathbf z}$ below; the normal points upward. Reconstruct the surface current. Compute its force per area both as $\mathbf K\times\mathbf B_{\rm avg}$ and as the upper-minus-lower jump of Maxwell traction. Next add the same uniform field $\mathbf C=C_t\hat{\mathbf x}+C_n\hat{\mathbf z}$ to both measured sides. Prove that this common mode leaves the reconstructed current unchanged but changes the load, and find that load change. Explain which extra global boundary, circulation, or flux data are needed to distinguish the two physical configurations and why a jump-only inverse cannot predict stress.
permittedResults: $\mathbf f/A=\mathbf K\times\mathbf B_{\rm avg}$ for an ideal sheet
problems.strategy: Separate measured data into jump and mean components before calculating force. Use the jump for surface current, the mean for Lorentz loading, reproduce both components from traction, and perturb only the mean to expose the inverse null space.
hints: The boundary law depends on $\mathbf B_+-\mathbf B_-$, whereas the sheet force depends on their arithmetic mean.
For each side, evaluate $\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}$ before taking the upper-minus-lower difference.
Under the common-mode addition, compute $\mathbf K\times\mathbf C$ rather than repeating the entire stress algebra.
problems.solution: The boundary law gives $\mathbf K=\hat{\mathbf z}\times(\mathbf B_+-\mathbf B_-)/\mu_0=[(B_+-B_-)/\mu_0]\hat{\mathbf y}$. With $\bar B_t=(B_++B_-)/2$, the average-field force is $\mathbf f/A=[(B_+-B_-)/\mu_0](B_n\hat{\mathbf x}-\bar B_t\hat{\mathbf z})$, equivalently $(B_+-B_-)B_n\hat{\mathbf x}/\mu_0-(B_+^2-B_-^2)\hat{\mathbf z}/(2\mu_0)$. Vacuum stress gives $\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}=[B_nB_t\hat{\mathbf x}+(B_n^2-B_t^2)\hat{\mathbf z}/2]/\mu_0$ on either side, and the upper-minus-lower traction reproduces the same two components. Adding $\mathbf C$ to both sides leaves their difference and therefore $\mathbf K$ invariant, but shifts the mean. The load changes by $\Delta(\mathbf f/A)=\mathbf K\times\mathbf C=[(B_+-B_-)/\mu_0](C_n\hat{\mathbf x}-C_t\hat{\mathbf z})$. Thus the local jump identifies the sheet source but not its mechanical loading. Remote boundary values, the tangential circulation around a noncontractible or enclosing contour, and the normal flux through a spanning surface can fix the common tangential and normal modes. Without such global data, two fields with identical local inverse-current evidence exert different stresses.
rubricCriteria: Reconstructs the signed surface current from jump data and separates jump from mean field.
Derives both load components by Lorentz force and independently by the Maxwell-traction jump.
Computes the common-mode load shift and identifies the global circulation or flux information missing from a jump-only inverse.

commonErrors.description: Uses one side's total field instead of the side average in the sheet Lorentz force.
commonErrors.consequence: The self-field is included asymmetrically, so the stress comparison and common-mode decomposition both fail.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that an unchanged field jump implies unchanged force.
commonErrors.consequence: The mean field that couples to the reconstructed current is discarded even though local boundary data do not fix it.

problems.flawedProof: Reconstruct the correct sheet current from the field jump, but compute its load with the upper-side field alone: $\mathbf f/A=\mathbf K\times\mathbf B_+$. A common added field still changes this one-sided load by $\mathbf K\times\mathbf C$.

problems.title: Linked flux classifies exterior vector potentials by topology
problems.objective: Prove that exterior curl-free vector potentials with different linked flux cannot be connected by a global single-valued gauge.
problems.statement: Remove a solid toroidal flux region from space and consider the connected exterior domain. Two vector potentials $\mathbf A_1$ and $\mathbf A_2$ have the same local magnetic field in the exterior but circulations $\Phi_1$ and $\Phi_2$ around a loop linking the torus once. Prove that a global single-valued gauge relates them if and only if $\Phi_1=\Phi_2$, assuming all nonlinking loop periods vanish.
permittedResults: Closed-loop period criterion for path independence
problems.strategy: Apply a hypothetical single-valued gauge to the linking generator to prove the necessary period condition. For sufficiency, build the scalar by path integration and use vanishing periods to establish path independence.
hints: Apply a hypothetical global gradient to the linking loop first.
For sufficiency, define chi by a path integral from a base point.
Use vanishing periods to prove the definition does not depend on the chosen path.
problems.solution:
Let $ oldsymbol\alpha=\mathbf A_2-\mathbf A_1$. Equal exterior B gives $
abla	imes oldsymbol\alpha=0$. If $ oldsymbol\alpha=
abla\chi$ for single-valued chi, every closed-loop integral vanishes, so in particular $\Phi_2-\Phi_1=0$; equality of linked periods is necessary. Conversely, in this one-handle exterior, a curl-free one-form whose period vanishes on the linking generator and on all contractible loops has zero period on every loop. Define $\chi(\mathbf r)=\int_{\mathbf r_0}^{\mathbf r} oldsymbol\alpha\cdot d oldsymbol\ell$; zero periods make it path independent and give $
abla\chi= oldsymbol\alpha$. Thus linked flux labels distinct global gauge classes even when local exterior fields agree.

Constructs the path-integral gauge under zero-period assumptions.
States the topology assumption and distinguishes local field equality from global gauge equivalence.

commonErrors.consequence: The noncontractible linking loop is omitted.

commonErrors.consequence: The proposed scalar can be multivalued by exactly the linked-flux difference.

problems.flawedProof: Equal curls always imply a global gradient, so any two exterior potentials are gauge equivalent even when their linking circulations differ.

problems.title: Design an azimuthal current that confines an axial field
problems.objective: Invert a prescribed compact axial magnetic profile into volume and surface current and verify field confinement.
problems.statement: Design a cylindrically symmetric current distribution that produces $\mathbf B=B_0(1-r^2/a^2)^2\hat{\mathbf z}$ for $r<a$ and zero B for $r\ge a$. Find the required volume current, determine whether a surface current is needed at r equal to a, and verify current continuity.
problems.strategy: Convert the prescribed axial field profile into azimuthal current with the relevant cylindrical curl component. Differentiate the taper, check regularity and boundary smoothness, and verify that the designed source confines the field without a hidden sheet.
hints: Use the phi component of curl B for an axial radial profile.
Differentiate the squared taper before assessing its endpoint.
Check both the tangential-field jump and divergence of the reconstructed J.
problems.solution: With axial B depending on r, Ampere law gives $J_\phi=-(1/\mu_0)dB_z/dr$. Differentiation yields $\mathbf J=[4B_0r/(\mu_0a^2)](1-r^2/a^2)\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$ for $r<a$. The field itself and its first derivative both vanish at r equal to a, so tangential B is continuous to zero and no delta-function surface current is required. The azimuthal current is divergence-free because it is independent of phi and has no radial or axial component. It also vanishes at the axis and boundary, forming closed current rings that confine the designed axial flux.
rubricCriteria: Derives the exact azimuthal volume-current profile and direction.
Correctly finds no surface-current sheet at the smooth boundary.
Verifies divergence-free closed rings and field confinement.

commonErrors.description: Uses positive dB z over dr for J phi.
commonErrors.consequence: The designed current produces the opposite axial-field gradient.

commonErrors.description: Adds a surface current merely because the material support ends.
commonErrors.consequence: The continuous zero tangential field has no jump requiring a sheet.

problems.flawedProof: The azimuthal curl relation is $\mathbf J=(dB_z/dr)\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}/\mu_0$. Because the tangential magnetic field reaches zero continuously at $r=a$, no surface sheet is added.

problems.title: Optimize a magnetic gap before core saturation
problems.objective: Optimize an actuator air gap at a fixed current limit while enforcing core saturation, then quantify the active-constraint and gap-dominated regimes.
problems.statement: An ideal magnetic circuit has core length $\ell_c$, permeability $\mu_c$, cross-sectional area $A$, one adjustable air gap constrained by $g\ge g_{\min}>0$, and $N$ turns. The drive is limited to $I_{\max}$, and the design must satisfy $B\le B_{\rm sat}$ at that current. Neglect leakage and fringing. Derive $B(g)$ and the attractive force at $I_{\max}$. Choose the feasible gap that maximizes force without exceeding saturation, giving the answer piecewise according to whether the saturation constraint is active above the manufacturing minimum. Find the maximum force in each case and compute $d\ln F/d\ln g$ in the gap-dominated unsaturated regime. State why the linear-core model cannot be used to gain more force by violating the constraint.
permittedResults: Ampere law along a magnetic circuit
Flux continuity in equal cross section
problems.strategy: Express the common induction through the sum of core and gap magnetomotive drops at the fixed current ceiling. Since force decreases monotonically with gap, combine the saturation-derived lower bound with the positive manufacturing minimum and distinguish the saturation-limited and manufacturing-limited branches.
hints: At fixed current, maximizing force is equivalent to maximizing B.
Combine $B(I_{\max},g)\le B_{\rm sat}$ with the manufacturing lower bound on g.
When $g/\mu_0$ dominates the core term, use $F\propto g^{-2}$ for logarithmic sensitivity.
problems.solution: Flux continuity makes B common, and Ampere law gives $NI_{\max}=B(\ell_c/\mu_c+g/\mu_0)$. Thus $B(g)=NI_{\max}/(\ell_c/\mu_c+g/\mu_0)$ and $F(g)=AB(g)^2/(2\mu_0)$. Saturation requires $g\ge g_{\rm sat}=\mu_0[NI_{\max}/B_{\rm sat}-\ell_c/\mu_c]$. Because F decreases with g, $g_{\rm opt}=\max\{g_{\min},g_{\rm sat}\}$. If $g_{\rm sat}>g_{\min}$, saturation is active, $B=B_{\rm sat}$, and $F_{\max}=AB_{\rm sat}^2/(2\mu_0)$. If $g_{\rm sat}\le g_{\min}$, the minimum manufacturable gap remains unsaturated and $F_{\max}=A[NI_{\max}/(\ell_c/\mu_c+g_{\min}/\mu_0)]^2/(2\mu_0)$. In the gap-dominated unsaturated regime, $B\simeq\mu_0NI_{\max}/g$ and $F\simeq A\mu_0N^2I_{\max}^2/(2g^2)$, so $d\ln F/d\ln g=-2$. Driving beyond $B_{\rm sat}$ invalidates constant $\mu_c$; the extrapolated quadratic force is not an admissible improvement.
rubricCriteria: Derives the exact field and force at the current ceiling and converts saturation into a gap inequality.
Obtains the piecewise optimal gap and corresponding maximum force.
Finds logarithmic sensitivity minus two in the gap-dominated regime and rejects post-saturation extrapolation.

commonErrors.consequence: A feasible but strictly weaker force is selected because force decreases with gap.

commonErrors.description: Uses the active-saturation formula when its required gap lies below the manufacturing minimum.
commonErrors.consequence: The feasible unsaturated branch at $g_{\min}$ is omitted.

problems.flawedProof: Magnetic force is proportional to the volume of the air gap. Therefore, after satisfying saturation, the force-maximizing design uses the largest available gap.

problems.title: Exterior silence hides an infinite family of current profiles
problems.objective: Construct two regular distributed currents with identical complete exterior data but different interior fields and energies, thereby exhibiting a nontrivial inverse-source null space.
problems.statement: An infinite coaxial source has an inner conductor $0<r<b$ carrying total current $+I$ and an ideal return sheet at $r=a>b$ carrying $-I$. Compare two admissible inner profiles: $\mathbf J_A=I\hat{\mathbf z}/(\pi b^2)$ and $\mathbf J_B=2I(1-r^2/b^2)\hat{\mathbf z}/(\pi b^2)$. Verify that both carry total I. Derive $\mathbf B(r)$ for each profile in $0<r<b$, $b<r<a$, and $r>a$. Show that every exterior magnetic measurement is identical even though the interior fields differ. Compute the magnetic energy per unit length inside the inner conductor for each case, identify the common annular energy, and state what additional measurements or prior constraints could make reconstruction unique.
problems.strategy: Normalize both current profiles and integrate their enclosed-current functions before applying Ampere's law. Their total currents force the same annular and exterior branches; integrating the distinct interior fields squared then supplies a quantitative witness that exterior equality does not imply source equality.
hints: For profile B, the enclosed fraction is $2r^2/b^2-r^4/b^4$.
After $r=b$, only total inner current matters until the return sheet is crossed.
Use $x=r/b$ to reduce the profile-B energy integral to a dimensionless polynomial.
problems.solution: Area integration gives $I_A(r)=Ir^2/b^2$ and $I_B(r)=I(2r^2/b^2-r^4/b^4)$ for $r<b$; both reach I at b. Hence $\mathbf B_A=\mu_0Ir\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}/(2\pi b^2)$ and $\mathbf B_B=(\mu_0I/2\pi)(2r/b^2-r^3/b^4)\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$ inside. For either profile, $\mathbf B=\mu_0I\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}/(2\pi r)$ in $b<r<a$, while crossing the return sheet reduces enclosed current to zero and gives $\mathbf B=\mathbf0$ for $r>a$. Thus the complete exterior field, not merely a finite set of moments, is identical. Direct energy integration yields $U'_{A,\rm inner}=\mu_0I^2/(16\pi)$ and $U'_{B,\rm inner}=11\mu_0I^2/(96\pi)$; for B the dimensionless integral is $\int_0^1x(2x-x^3)^2dx=11/24$. Both share $U'_{\rm annulus}=\mu_0I^2\ln(a/b)/(4\pi)$. Interior field probes, spatially resolved current data, internal energy or inductance measurements, a known constitutive current law with terminal voltage, or a finite-dimensional profile prior can distinguish the sources. Exterior magnetostatic data alone leave an infinite radial-profile null space.
rubricCriteria: Normalizes both profiles and derives their distinct regular interior fields plus common outer branches.
Computes both inner-conductor energies and the shared annular contribution.
Proves complete exterior nonuniqueness and identifies data or priors that remove the radial-profile null space.

commonErrors.description: Uses total I at every radius inside either conductor.
commonErrors.consequence: Both regular distributed fields are replaced by a singular inverse-radius branch.

commonErrors.description: Concludes identical exterior fields imply identical magnetic energies.
commonErrors.consequence: The unobserved inner-conductor contribution, which depends on radial profile, is discarded.

problems.flawedProof: Use the full current I as enclosed at every positive radius inside either conductor. Both interior fields are then $B_\phi=\mu_0I/(2\pi r)$; imposing the same microscopic radial cutoff gives equal inner energies, followed by the common annular and zero exterior branches.
